MapMaker lessons: Grade 8 US History

Ten lessons that teach Grade 8 US History with National Geographic MapMaker maps, arranged by topic in the order most courses teach them. Each one pairs a map with an inquiry, a Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and a separate teacher page with the answers.

12 lessons · US History · no account or login needed

Road to revolution and the Revolution

  • 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

    Grade 8 · About 62 minutes: 52 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15

    Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

Confederation and the Constitution

  • Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

    Grade 8 · About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15 · also fits: The early republic

    Map the public places in your own community where people use the rights in the Bill of Rights and carry out their responsibilities as citizens, and find who represents your district in Congress.

  • We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

    Grade 8 · About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15 · also fits: The early republic

    See how House seats were shared out after the 1790 census, how the three-fifths clause changed the count, and how close each state's vote to ratify was.

The early republic

  • The First Political Parties, 1796–1800

    Grade 8 · About 57 minutes: 47 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15

    Compare how each state's electors voted in 1796 and 1800, see which states changed sides, and work out whether one state decided the election of 1800.

  • The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

    Grade 8 · About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15 · also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Compare the Louisiana Purchase with the United States of 1803, see why the Mississippi River and New Orleans mattered, and follow Lewis and Clark's route across rivers and biomes to the Pacific.

  • The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

    Grade 8 · About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15 · also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

Age of Jackson

  • Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894

    Grade 8 · About 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question · also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

    Turn on one period at a time to watch American Indian land cessions spread across the United States, predict where the next ones will be, and explain why the 1830s cessions are where they are. The map is Charles Royce's record of cessions, so students also ask whose view it shows.

  • The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote

    Grade 8 · About 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question

    See how each state's electors voted in 1828, then turn on who could vote there: the property and tax rules for white men, and whether free Black men could vote. Students test the idea that Jackson's election was a victory for the common man against the rules state by state.

Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

  • Roads, Trails, and Rails West

    Grade 8 · About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15 · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

Reform and the road to war

  • US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850

    Grade 8 · About 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    Start with where slavery was legal in late 1850 and the line Congress drew in 1820. Then turn on, one layer at a time, the routes along which enslaved people were sold south, two ships whose captives took control, and the routes people followed to escape.

The Civil War

  • Civil War Battlefields

    Grade 8 · About 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question · also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration

    Start with the 35 states of 1863 shaded by side, predict where the fighting happened, then turn on the battlefields and the railroads to test the prediction. Students use the pop-ups and Measure to explain why so much of the war was fought in a few places.

  • The Battle of Vicksburg

    Grade 8 · About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15

    Follow Grant's 1863 march to Vicksburg along the Mississippi River, and see why taking the city split the Confederacy in two.

In every lesson

  • A MapMaker map that opens straight from the page, with each layer’s source listed. No account or login is needed.
  • An inquiry with a compelling question and questions you can pick from, each answered from the map.
  • A Word student sheet in English and Spanish that you can edit, print or open in Google Docs.
  • A separate answer page, and a Word file, with where to find each answer on the map and what to accept.
  • Links to how-to videos, a link to Vera, and a prompt for your own AI tool.

How these lessons work: materials, preparing, and ways to run a lesson.

Make your own questions

Vera, the Support Hub’s AI assistant, has every lesson’s map, bookmarks, layers and questions, but not the answers. Name a lesson and ask for easier or harder questions, a short quiz, questions for your own state’s standards or questions in another language. Each lesson page also has a prompt you can paste into another AI tool.

Ask Vera (opens in a new tab)

Vera’s questions aren’t reviewed like these lessons. Each one should be answerable from the map; if one isn’t, please tell us using Report a problem on the lesson page.

settings.markdown:
Lessons

How these lessons work

What every MapMaker lesson includes, how to prepare, and ways to run one.

What every lesson includes

  • Each lesson is one MapMaker map and a set of questions that students answer by using the map: opening bookmarks, clicking pop-ups, reading the legend, turning layers on and off and measuring. The questions can't be answered from a textbook alone.
  • Students need no account or login. Open in MapMaker opens the map straight from the lesson page; the Share to Google Classroom button shares the map link with a class.
  • The Word student sheet (English and Spanish) is two pages: a big question, some background, help reading the map, the questions with space to write, and a closing reflection. Print it or share it digitally; it opens in Word and Google Docs.
  • Each lesson page lists the questions with the exact steps for the front of the class, marks one question as the one to use if you only have 15 minutes, and gives ideas for support and stretch.
  • Where to find each answer on the map, and what to accept, are on a separate answer page and in the Word teacher notes, so the lesson page can be shared with students.
  • Sketches on the map are not saved between sessions. Students who sketch should finish in one session or take a screenshot.
  • Vera, the Support Hub's AI assistant, knows every lesson's map, layers and questions but not the answers. Each lesson page also has a prompt to paste into another AI tool, which lists the map's layers so the tool doesn't invent any.

Ways to run a lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Materials

The lesson includes the MapMaker map, a two-page Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and these teacher notes. Print the sheet, or download it and upload it to Google Drive to edit it in Google Docs (it also opens in Word). The Google Classroom button shares the map, not the sheet; to assign the sheet, attach your Drive copy in Classroom with Make a copy for each student, or paste the map link and attach the sheet yourself. No account or login is needed. Sketches on the map are not saved between sessions.

Preparing

  • Open the map and click through the bookmarks and pop-ups. Check the legend at the zoom levels the questions use; it changes as you zoom and as layers are turned on and off.
  • Decide whether students work alone, in pairs or as a whole class, and whether they use the printed sheet or a digital copy.
  • Encourage students to look for patterns and make observations, not just to find the right answers.
  • Layers the questions don't use are there for further study.

Assessing the answer to the big question

Every lesson ends with students answering the compelling question with evidence from the map. This rubric is one way to assess that answer; each lesson's answer page adds a line on what counts as map evidence for that map, and a model answer. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

Help

Short how-to videos for every MapMaker tool are on the MapMaker Educator Support Hub (opens in a new tab). Each lesson page has a Report a problem button that tells us which lesson you mean.

Lessons › US History › Road to revolution and the Revolution

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Explore how the geography of North America shaped the first two years of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington and Concord to Washington's attack on Trenton.

  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 62 minutes: 52 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicRoad to revolution and the Revolution
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • TX 8.4(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.6

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Share to Google Classroom (opens in a new tab) Student sheet Teacher notes

Open in MapMaker: (opens in a new tab)

The map as it opens.

Inquiry

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Where did the war begin? About 10 minutes

    Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then the Boston diamond. Read the dates in each pop-up, and the winner from the diamond's color and the legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    From the front

    1. Open the Massachusetts bookmark.
    2. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord and read the date line.
    3. Open the legend and find which color means an American victory.
    4. Ask: who won, and how do you know from the map?
    5. Click the Boston diamond and read its two dates.
    6. Ask: how long did the siege of Boston last?
    7. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.
    8. Ask: how close to Boston did the war begin?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776? If you only do one About 15 minutes

    Zoom out one step from the Massachusetts bookmark and drag the map from Quebec to South Carolina to find all 21 diamonds (they disappear if you zoom out too far). Click each one, read its dates, and sort the battles into two lists by year. Use the legend for the winner. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

    From the front

    1. Zoom out one step from the Massachusetts bookmark and drag the map from Quebec to South Carolina to show all 21 diamonds. If they disappear, zoom in one step.
    2. Click the Bunker Hill diamond and read the date line.
    3. Click the Brooklyn diamond and read the date line.
    4. Open the legend and check the color of each of those two diamonds.
    5. Ask: which colonies had battles in 1775, and which in 1776?
    6. Ask: where did the fighting move to, and who was winning there?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Why New York? About 15 minutes

    Turn on Key Port Cities in Map layers. Students use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port, click the major ports between Boston and Charleston to read their names, measure New York to Philadelphia and New York to Boston, and say what a navy based at New York could reach.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781.
    2. Open the legend and show the larger symbol for a Major Port City and the smaller one for a Port.
    3. Ask: Boston and Charleston are major ports; which other major ports lie between them?
    4. Use Measure from New York to Philadelphia.
    5. Use Measure from New York to Boston.
    6. Ask: what could a navy based at New York reach?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. How did 1776 end? About 12 minutes

    Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and read the dates and the winner from the legend. Measure the distance from the Brooklyn diamond (New York City) to Trenton.

    From the front

    1. Zoom in on New York City until the numbered Turning Points circles appear.
    2. Click circle 4 and read the Battle details text.
    3. Click the diamond for Fort Lee and read its dates. Circle 4 covers the Fort Washington diamond: click the circle and use the arrow in the pop-up (2 of 2) to reach the battle.
    4. Click circle 5, read its Battle details text, then use the arrow in the pop-up (2 of 2) to reach the Trenton battle and read its date.
    5. Zoom out until the circles disappear, open the legend and check the color of each diamond.
    6. Use Measure for the distance from the Brooklyn diamond (New York City) to Trenton.
    7. Ask: how far from New York City had the fighting moved, and how did 1776 end for Washington's army?

    Tools: Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch (not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot), or a short talk using the bookmark and the layers.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. To edit it, download it and upload it to Google Drive (it opens in Google Docs) or open it in Word. Students need no account or login.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

The Share to Google Classroom button at the top of the page shares the MapMaker map with a class, not the sheet. To assign the sheet, attach your Drive copy in Classroom and choose Make a copy for each student.

1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

Open the map in MapMaker: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Before you start

British soldiers marched out of Boston to seize weapons that colonists had stored at Concord. The fighting that followed started the American Revolution. For the next two years, the British army and navy and the new Continental Army, led by George Washington, fought over the colonies' cities, rivers and harbors.

Reading the map

Diamonds mark battles. A battle's pop-up gives its name, dates and story, but not the winner in words: the diamond's color shows the winner, so use the legend. Each diamond is placed at the battle's usual location, but the fighting covered a wider area: gray shaded areas show the battlefield, and areas with diagonal stripes show the core, where the fighting was heaviest. Zoom in to see white numbered circles: five turning points, numbered in the order they happened. In the Key Port Cities layer, click a port to see its name; the legend tells a major port from a smaller one.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the war begin?

    On the map:

    1. Open the Massachusetts bookmark.
    2. Click the diamond at Lexington and Concord and read its dates.
    3. Open the legend and check which color shows who won.
    4. Click the Boston diamond and read its dates.
    5. Use Measure for the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

    Answer: When was Lexington and Concord fought, and who won? How long did the siege of Boston last? How close to Boston did the war begin? Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord: miles

  2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

    On the map:

    1. Zoom out one step from the Massachusetts bookmark. Drag the map from Quebec in the north to South Carolina in the south to find all 21 diamonds. If the diamonds disappear, you have zoomed out too far: zoom in one step.
    2. Click the diamonds and read each one's date line to see its year.
    3. Read the colony's name printed on the map under each group of diamonds (colonies have no pop-up, and Quebec is not labeled). Use the legend to see who won.

    Answer: Which colonies had battles in 1775? Which in 1776? What changed?

  3. Why New York?

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781.
    2. Use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port.
    3. Find the major ports between Boston and Charleston.
    4. Click each major port to read its name in the pop-up.
    5. Use Measure from New York to Philadelphia and from New York to Boston.

    Answer: Boston and Charleston are major ports: which other major ports lie between them? Using the distances you measured, what could a navy based at New York reach? New York to Philadelphia: miles. New York to Boston: miles

  4. How did 1776 end?

    On the map:

    1. Zoom in on New York City until the numbered circles appear.
    2. Follow circles 4 and 5.
    3. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton. A numbered circle covers the Fort Washington and Trenton diamonds: click the circle and use the arrow in the pop-up to reach the battle (2 of 2).
    4. Read each one's dates, and use the legend to see who won. To see the color of a covered diamond, zoom out until the circles disappear.
    5. Use Measure for the distance from the Brooklyn diamond (New York City) to Trenton.

    Answer: When was each battle fought, and who won? How far from New York City had the fighting moved by the end of 1776? Measure the distance from New York City to Trenton: miles

Your answer: Answer the big question in a short paragraph. Name at least two places on the map, and give a date or a distance for each.

Looking back

Trenton is one small American win after a run of British ones. Why do you think the map gives it its own turning point?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Social Studies. Grade: 8. Time: About 62 minutes: 52 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Locate the 21 battles of 1775–1776 on the map and sort them by year, using the pop-up dates and the legend for the winner.
  • Measure straight-line distances between Boston, Concord, New York, Philadelphia and Trenton with the Measure tool.
  • Identify the major ports between Boston and Charleston from the Key Port Cities layer and the coastline, and explain what a navy based at New York could reach.
  • Trace the end of 1776 through the numbered Turning Points and the Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton pop-ups.
  • Use evidence from at least two places on the map to explain why the fighting moved from Boston to New York and across New Jersey.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Reading pop-ups
  • Using a map legend
  • Measuring distances on a map
  • Navigating a map
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Sketching on a map

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: Every layer is on when the map opens except Key Port Cities, which students turn on for question 3. The Massachusetts bookmark takes students to the first battles. Question 2 goes faster if each pair takes the diamonds in one region (New England and Quebec, New York and New Jersey, or the South) and the class combines the lists.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. Looking at where the 1775 battles cluster and where the 1776 battles cluster, what does the map suggest about each side's plan for the war?
  2. The Key Port Cities layer has no pop-ups, so you had to work out the ports from the coastline and the battle diamonds. What other clues on the map helped, and what was missing?
  3. Nearly every 1776 battle around New York was a British victory, yet the year ends with Trenton. Using the distances you measured, why might that one small battle have mattered so much?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do question 1 together from the front and write the two diamond colors and what each means on the board before students start question 2.
  • Stretch: Find the 1763 Proclamation Line and ask whether any of the 21 battles were fought west of it, and what that says about where the war was being fought.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The early war was fought in Massachusetts.” By the end of 1776 the map shows battles in seven colonies and in Quebec.
  • “The winner is the side that lost fewer soldiers.” Bunker Hill is shown as a British victory, yet its pop-up says the British had twice as many casualties as the Patriots.
  • “The Americans lost every battle in 1776.” The map shows American wins in the South that year, such as Moores Creek Bridge and Sullivan's Island, as well as Trenton.

Key words

  • siege
  • militia
  • Continental Army
  • Loyalist
  • harbor
  • campaign
  • retreat

Further reading

  • MapMaker: American Revolution: 1775-1776 (New England/New York) (opens in a new tab) (National Geographic Education)
  • MapMaker: American Revolution: 1777-1778 (Mid-Atlantic) (opens in a new tab) (National Geographic Education)
  • History & Culture, Minute Man National Historical Park (opens in a new tab) (National Park Service)

Answers

Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept are kept off this page, so it can be shared with students: answer notes (web page) or Download Word (teacher notes). The answer page also has a rubric for the answer to the compelling question and a model answer.

About this map

This map follows the first two years of the American Revolution, 1775 and 1776. It shows 21 battles from those years and the land their battlefields covered, against the colony borders of 1763 and the 1763 Proclamation Line. Five numbered turning points, which appear when you zoom in, mark the order of events from Lexington and Concord to Trenton. A layer of port cities, off when the map opens, adds the ports that supplied armies and moved troops.

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Revolutionary War BattlesWhat it shows: 21 battles from April 1775 to December 1776. Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates, a picture and a short account. The winner is shown only by the diamond's color, as listed in the legend (American Victory or British Victory); the pop-up does not state it in words.Source: American Battlefield Trust
Revolutionary War BattlefieldsWhat it shows: Battlefield boundaries (gray) and the core areas where the fighting was heaviest (diagonal stripes). No pop-ups.Source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Turning PointsWhat it shows: Five white circles numbered 1 to 5, from Lexington and Concord to Trenton, that appear when you zoom in. Each pop-up gives the event's name, year, a short account (the Battle_details field) and the victor.Source: Chris Bunin and Peter Trentacoste (2026), from National Park Service, US Army Center of Military History and Library of Congress sources
Thirteen British ColoniesWhat it shows: Colony areas and borders in 1763, with each colony's name printed on the map. Colonies have no pop-up.Source: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988)
1763 Proclamation LineWhat it shows: The line west of which King George III barred colonial settlement and land purchases, reserving the land beyond it for American Indian nationsSource: National Geographic Society and Virginia Geographic Alliance, from the Historical Atlas of the United States (1988); the reservation is in the Proclamation's text (Avalon Project, Yale Law School (opens in a new tab))
Key Port Cities in the American Revolution 1775-1781 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Ports that supplied armies and moved troops, from New England to the Caribbean and Britain. The legend separates a Major Port City (larger symbol) from a smaller Port. settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History › Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny

Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.

  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicWestward expansion and Manifest Destiny (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.11(A)
    • TX 8.6(B)
    • TX 8.6(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.4.1

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Share to Google Classroom (opens in a new tab) Student sheet Teacher notes

Open in MapMaker: (opens in a new tab)

The map as it opens.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Where did the trails begin? About 10 minutes

    Click three trails (use the legend to tell them apart) and note from each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?

    From the front

    1. Open the legend and show the seven trail colors.
    2. Click the dotted Oregon trail line and read where it started and ended.
    3. Click the Santa Fe trail and read where it started.
    4. Click the Pony Express trail and read where it started.
    5. Ask: in which state do most of the trails start?
    6. Ask: looking at the map, why there?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. How far, and how many? About 12 minutes

    Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri (on the basemap, just east of Kansas City), to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.

    From the front

    1. Click the Oregon trail line in Idaho or Oregon, where it runs alone, and read its length and how many people used it.
    2. Zoom in on Kansas City and find Independence, Missouri, on the basemap.
    3. Use Measure in miles from Independence to Portland, Oregon.
    4. Ask: how much longer is the trail than the straight line?
    5. Trace the dotted Oregon line from Independence to Portland with the pointer.
    6. Ask: why is the trail so much longer than a straight line?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Whose land? If you only do one About 15 minutes

    Turn on Indigenous Territories in Map layers and zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail from end to end. Was the West empty land when the trails were built? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories.
    2. Zoom in until the nations' names appear along the Oregon trail.
    3. Trace the Oregon trail from Independence to Portland, reading out the names it crosses.
    4. Ask: was the land the trail crossed empty?
    5. Ask: what might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. From trails to rails About 12 minutes

    Turn on the Railroads group in Map layers. Using the legend, which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line near a trail, read when it was in operation, and compare the year with 1869, when the California Trail stopped being used (the thick transcontinental lines have no pop-up).

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on Railroads.
    2. Open the legend and find Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific).
    3. Trace the two thick lines from Omaha to Sacramento.
    4. Ask: which dotted trails do they follow most closely?
    5. Click a thin gray railroad line near a trail and read the year it was in operation by.
    6. Ask: was that before or after 1869, and what happened to the wagon trails once the railroad opened?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, one journey sketched on the map with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab)

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the spatial connections among human settlements and affect the diffusion of ideas and cultural practices
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.11(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze how physical characteristics of the environment influenced population distribution, settlement patterns, and economic activities in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.6(B)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Explain the political, economic, and social roots of Manifest Destiny
TX 8.6(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the relationship between the concept of Manifest Destiny and the westward growth of the nation
FL SS.8.A.4.1Framework: FloridaStandard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness

National frameworks first, then state examples. For your own state's standards, ask Vera or use the prompt under Make your own questions.

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. To edit it, download it and upload it to Google Drive (it opens in Google Docs) or open it in Word. Students need no account or login.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

The Share to Google Classroom button at the top of the page shares the MapMaker map with a class, not the sheet. To assign the sheet, attach your Drive copy in Classroom and choose Make a copy for each student.

Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

Open the map in MapMaker: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Before you start

In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people from the eastern United States went west in wagons, looking for farmland, gold or a place to practice their religion freely. A journey along one of the trails could take months. Later in the century, railroads were built across the West.

Reading the map

Each trail is a dotted line in its own color; the legend names them, and clicking a trail opens its pop-up. City and state names are part of the basemap. Railroads and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens: turn them on in Map layers. Thick colored lines are the transcontinental railroads, named in the legend, and thin gray lines are other railroads; of the railroads, only the thin gray lines have pop-ups. Each Indigenous nation's territory is shaded in its own color; its name appears when you zoom in, or when you click the shading. The territories are approximate and aren't listed in the legend.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where did the trails begin?

    On the map:

    1. Open the legend to see which color is which trail.
    2. Click three of the dotted trail lines.
    3. Read in each pop-up where the trail started and ended.

    Answer: Where did each trail start? In which state do most of them start, and why there? Use the Missouri River on the map.

  2. How far, and how many?

    On the map:

    1. Find the Oregon Trail's color in the legend.
    2. Click the Oregon Trail and read its length and how many people traveled it. Check that the pop-up's title says Oregon Trail: where trails share a route, another trail may open first, so use the arrow or click the line in Idaho or Oregon.
    3. Find Independence, Missouri, on the basemap, next to Kansas City.
    4. Use Measure for a straight line from Independence to Portland, Oregon.

    Answer: How long was the Oregon Trail, and how many people traveled it? Why is the trail longer than a straight line? Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: miles

  3. Whose land?

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories.
    2. Zoom in until the nations' names appear.
    3. Follow one trail from one end to the other.
    4. Find two nations whose land it crossed: read the names on the map or click the shading.

    Answer: Which two nations' land did the trail cross? Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

  4. From trails to rails

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Railroads.
    2. Use the legend to find the Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines.
    3. Click a thin gray railroad line near one of the trails and read when it was in operation by.

    Answer: Which trails do the Transcontinental Railroad lines follow most closely? Was your gray line in operation before or after 1869, when the California Trail stopped being used? What does that suggest?

Your answer: Answer the big question from two points of view: a settler on a trail, and a nation whose land it crossed. Use the map for both.

Looking back

Pick one nation whose land a trail crossed. What would you want to ask someone who lived there in 1850?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Indigenous Studies, Economics. Grade: 8. Time: About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Identify where three of the seven trails started and ended from their pop-ups, and explain from the map why most began in Missouri.
  • Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the Oregon Trail's length in its pop-up.
  • Name Indigenous nations whose lands a trail crossed, using the Indigenous Territories layer.
  • Compare the transcontinental railroad lines in the legend with the dotted trails to see which routes the railroads followed.
  • Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how trails and then railroads changed the West, and for whom.

Map skills

  • Reading pop-ups
  • Using a map legend
  • Measuring distances on a map
  • Navigating a map
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Sketching on a map

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: The Railroads group and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens; students turn them on in Map layers for questions 3 and 4. There are no bookmarks, so students zoom and pan to the trails themselves.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. The Oregon Trail is about 500 miles longer than the straight line you measured. What did the dotted line follow instead, and what does that say about what a wagon party needed most?
  2. With Indigenous Territories turned on, how did the map change for you? What might a trail have meant for the people whose lands it crossed, and whose story does the Trails West layer leave out?
  3. The Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines run close to the California and Mormon Pioneer trails. Why might the railroad builders have chosen the same route, and what happened to the trails once the railroad opened?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do question 1 together from the front, and write the seven trail names with their legend colors on the board so students can find each line.
  • Stretch: With Indigenous Territories and Railroads both on, ask whether the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line crosses the same nations' lands as the trails, and what that meant for those nations.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The West was empty before settlers arrived.” The Indigenous Territories layer shows nations' lands across the whole region the trails crossed.
  • “Everyone went west on the Oregon Trail.” The map shows seven trails, to Oregon, California, Utah, New Mexico and Southern California.
  • “The Pony Express lasted for decades.” Its pop-up says it ran for 18 months, from April 1860 to October 1861.

Key words

  • Manifest Destiny
  • emigrant
  • trail
  • transcontinental railroad
  • telegraph
  • Indigenous nation

Further reading

  • Tracking Growth in the U.S. (opens in a new tab) (National Geographic Education)
  • History & Culture, Oregon National Historic Trail (opens in a new tab) (National Park Service)
  • Primary Source Set: Westward Expansion: Encounters at a Cultural Crossroads (opens in a new tab) (Library of Congress)

Answers

Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept are kept off this page, so it can be shared with students: answer notes (web page) or Download Word (teacher notes). The answer page also has a rubric for the answer to the compelling question and a model answer.

About this map

This map shows the main routes west in the 1800s: seven overland trails, including the Oregon, California and Santa Fe Trails and the Pony Express. Two railroad layers, off when the map opens, show every line built from 1826 to 1911 and the five transcontinental lines completed by 1911, so the trails can be compared with the railroads. A layer of approximate Indigenous territories from a community-made map, also off at first, can be compared with the trails and railroads.

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Trails WestWhat it shows: Seven trails west: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish, Santa Fe, Butterfield Overland and Pony Express, each a dotted line in its own color in the legend. Each pop-up is titled with the trail's name and gives a short history with places, dates and distances.Source: National Geographic Education, from National Park Service trail information
Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Five transcontinental lines as thick colored lines named in the legend: Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific), Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) and Southern Pacific. No pop-up. In the Railroads group.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Railroads 1826 to 1911 (off when the map opens)What it shows: All railroad lines built from 1826 to 1911, as thin gray lines. Each pop-up gives the railroad's name (where recorded) and the year it was in operation by. In the Railroads group.Source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team
Indigenous Territories (off when the map opens)What it shows: Approximate territories of Indigenous nations, from a community-made map, each shaded in its own color with the nation's name appearing when zoomed in. Not listed in the legend. Click a territory to read the nation's name in the pop-up.Source: Native Land Digital

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History › Reform and the road to war

US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850

Start with where slavery was legal in late 1850 and the line Congress drew in 1820. Then turn on, one layer at a time, the routes along which enslaved people were sold south, two ships whose captives took control, and the routes people followed to escape.

  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question
  • TopicReform and the road to war (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.2

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Share to Google Classroom (opens in a new tab) Student sheet Teacher notes

Open in MapMaker: (opens in a new tab)

The map as it opens.

Inquiry

Compelling question

By 1850, how did slavery divide the United States, and what did that division mean for the people who were enslaved?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Four groups About 8 minutes

    With only the opening layers on, students read the legend, place a few states and territories in their groups, and find what New Jersey's pop-up adds to the word free.

    From the front

    1. Open The United States in 1850 bookmark and open the legend.
    2. Read the four groups aloud: free state, free territory, slave state (and Washington, D.C.), territory open to slavery.
    3. Ask: where are the dark orange states, and where are the dark blue ones?
    4. Click California, then Texas, and read the group and the year in each pop-up.
    5. Click New Jersey. Ask: it is shaded as a free state. What does its pop-up add?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. A line drawn in 1820 About 9 minutes

    Students read the dashed line's pop-up, then find one place that breaks its rule on each side of the year 1850: Missouri, and Utah Territory.

    From the front

    1. Click the dashed line and read its year and description.
    2. Ask: north of this line, what was supposed to be true?
    3. Click Missouri and read the note. Ask: which side of the line is most of Missouri on, and which group is it in?
    4. Click Unorganized territory, then Utah Territory. Ask: both are north of the line's latitude. Why are they in different groups?
    5. Point out where the dashed line stops in the west.

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  3. Before the routes appear About 5 minutes

    Before any route layer is on, students write down where they think enslaved people were being sold from and to inside the United States, and why.

    From the front

    1. Open The South bookmark. Keep the route layers off.
    2. Say: inside the slave states, enslaved people were sold and moved from one region to another.
    3. Ask: from which part of the orange states, and toward which part? What makes you think so? Have students write it down before any layer is turned on.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. Sold south If you only do one About 10 minutes

    Students turn on the slave trade routes, read the direction and account for the land and sea routes, and compare what they see with what they wrote in question 3.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on Routes of the slave trade within the United States.
    2. Open The South bookmark.
    3. Click a black line on land and read Direction people were moved and the account under it.
    4. Click a black line at sea and do the same.
    5. Ask: the lines have no arrows. Where do they start, where do many of them meet, and how do you know which way people were moved?
    6. Ask: how does this compare with what you wrote in question 3?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  5. Two ships About 8 minutes

    Students turn on the two ship routes and compare where each voyage ended and what happened to the people on board.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841).
    2. Open The United States in 1850 bookmark.
    3. Click the dashed purple line that runs up the Atlantic coast and read its pop-up.
    4. Click the shorter dashed purple line and read its pop-up.
    5. Ask: where did each voyage end, and who decided what happened to the people on board?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  6. Routes of escape About 10 minutes

    Students swap the trade routes for the Underground Railroad layers, follow the routes north, find the cities in Canada and measure how far beyond the Ohio River one route runs.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn off Routes of the slave trade within the United States and Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841). Turn on Underground Railroad approximate routes and Underground Railroad cities.
    2. Open The Ohio River and the North bookmark.
    3. Ask: which way do the green lines run, compared with the black lines in question 4?
    4. Click dots near the top of the map until you find a city in Canada.
    5. Use Measure to draw a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, on the Ohio River, to Chatham, in Canada. Chatham is the dot just east of Detroit; click it to check.
    6. Ask: Ohio was a free state. Why might a route keep going this far past it?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  7. What this map leaves out About 5 minutes

    Students read what the Underground Railroad pop-up says about its own routes and consider what a map drawn from an atlas of 1920 can and can't show.

    From the front

    1. Click any green line and read its pop-up.
    2. Ask: why are these routes only approximate?
    3. Ask: the map shows where routes ran. What does it not tell you about the people who were moved along them, or who escaped?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least three layers and two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised for them. Accept answers that describe the division on the map (free states in the North and California, free territories in the North and Northwest, slave states in the South, and Utah, New Mexico and Indian Territory open to slavery, with the line of 1820 and the exceptions of Missouri and Utah Territory) and say what it meant for enslaved people: being sold south and west along the trade routes, and escaping north, in many cases as far as Canada. Strong answers use New Jersey or the distance to Canada to show that free did not mean safe.

Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
FL SS.8.A.5.2Framework: FloridaStandard: Analyze the role of slavery in the development of sectional conflict

US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: By 1850, how did slavery divide the United States, and what did that division mean for the people who were enslaved?

Open the map in MapMaker: US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850

Before you start

In 1850 slavery was legal in some states and banned in others. A territory was land that belonged to the United States but was not yet a state. Twice, in 1820 and in 1850, Congress passed a compromise, an agreement where each side gives something up, about where slavery would be allowed. People who were enslaved were bought and sold, and many were forced to move far from their families. Some escaped. This map is traced from an atlas printed in 1920.

Reading the map

Dark blue: free state. Light blue: free territory. Dark orange: slave state, and Washington, D.C. Light orange: territory open to slavery. The dashed gray line is the Missouri Compromise line. Only these two layers are on at the start; turn on the others in Map layers when a question asks. Black lines are slave trade routes, dashed purple lines are two ships, green lines and black dots are the Underground Railroad. No line has arrows: click it and the pop-up gives the direction. Small states may have no name on the map; click one to see it.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Four groups

    On the map:

    1. Open The United States in 1850 bookmark and open the legend.
    2. Click California, Texas, Oregon Territory and New Mexico Territory. Read the group at the top of each pop-up.
    3. Click New Jersey and read the sentence under its group.

    Answer: (a) Which group is each of these in: California, Texas, Oregon Territory, New Mexico Territory? (b) In which part of the country are the slave states? (c) New Jersey is shaded as a free state. What does its pop-up say about people still held there in 1850?

  2. A line drawn in 1820

    On the map:

    1. Click the dashed line. Read the year and the description.
    2. Click Missouri and read the note at the bottom of its pop-up.
    3. Click Unorganized territory and then Utah Territory. Read the reason in each pop-up.
    4. Look at where the dashed line ends in the west.

    Answer: (a) What did the line of 1820 decide? (b) How is Missouri an exception to it? (c) Unorganized territory and Utah Territory are both north of the line's latitude. Which law decided about slavery in each one, and what did it say?

  3. Before the routes appear

    On the map:

    1. Open The South bookmark. Leave the other layers off.
    2. Write your idea down before you turn anything on.

    Answer: Inside the slave states, enslaved people were sold from one region to another. Which way do you think most of them were moved, and what makes you think so? I think most were moved from toward because .

  4. Sold south

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Routes of the slave trade within the United States.
    2. Open The South bookmark.
    3. Click a black line on land. Read Direction people were moved and the account under it.
    4. Click a black line at sea and read its pop-up too.

    Answer: (a) In which direction were enslaved people moved, by land and by sea? (b) Name two states the pop-up gives as places people were taken from, and the kind of country they were taken to. (c) Near which city or state do many of the lines meet? (d) Was your idea in question 3 right?

  5. Two ships

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Ships La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841).
    2. Open The United States in 1850 bookmark.
    3. Click each dashed purple line and read its pop-up.

    Answer: (a) Where did La Amistad start, and where did it end up? (b) Where was the Creole going, and where did the people on board take it instead? (c) What happened to the people on each ship in the end?

  6. Routes of escape

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn off the two route layers from questions 4 and 5. Turn on Underground Railroad approximate routes and Underground Railroad cities.
    2. Open The Ohio River and the North bookmark.
    3. Click the dots north of the Great Lakes and along the St. Lawrence River. Read the country in each pop-up.
    4. Use Measure to draw a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, in Canada. Chatham is the dot just east of Detroit; click it to check.

    Answer: (a) Which way do these routes run, compared with the slave trade routes? (b) Name the three cities in Canada. (c) About how far is it in a straight line from Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, Canada? (d) Ohio was a free state. What does that distance suggest about how safe a free state was for someone who had escaped? Ripley, Ohio, to Chatham, Canada: about miles

  7. What this map leaves out

    On the map:

    1. Click any green line and read its pop-up.
    2. Think about what you could count or name on this map, and what you could not.

    Answer: (a) Why does the pop-up call these routes approximate? (b) Name one thing about the people on these routes that the map does not show. (c) What other kind of source would help you find it out?

Your answer: Answer the big question, By 1850, how did slavery divide the United States, and what did that division mean for the people who were enslaved?, with evidence from at least three layers and two pop-ups. Then write one "why" question this map leaves you with.

Looking back

Which layer changed your picture of 1850 the most when you turned it on, and what did it add?

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Civics, Social Studies. Grade: 8. Time: About 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Use the legend and pop-ups to place states and territories of late 1850 in four groups, and read the reason given for each.
  • Explain what the Missouri Compromise line decided, and how Missouri and Utah Territory differ from its rule.
  • Test an idea about the direction of the slave trade within the United States against the routes and their pop-ups.
  • Follow the routes of La Amistad, the Creole and the Underground Railroad, and use a measured distance as evidence about safety in free states.
  • Say what a map drawn from a 1920 atlas can and can't show about the people on these routes.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Using a map legend
  • Reading pop-ups
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Measuring distances on a map

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: The map opens with only the states and territories and the Missouri Compromise line on. Students turn on the slave trade routes in question 4, the two ships in question 5 and the Underground Railroad layers in question 6, where the earlier route layers go off so the green lines stand out. Question 3's idea is best written down before any route layer is on. The subject is the buying, selling and forced movement of people, and some students may have family histories connected to it; the questions ask what the map shows and avoid asking students to imagine themselves enslaved or to defend slavery. The pop-ups use the terms enslaved people and people escaping slavery. Question 6 uses Measure; a straight line from Ripley to Chatham is enough.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. In question 3 you wrote where you thought enslaved people were moved. What was your idea based on, and what did the routes change?
  2. The trade routes run south and west and the escape routes run north. What does putting the two on one map show that either one alone would not?
  3. Two territories in 1850 were left for settlers to decide. What might follow from leaving that question open?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Questions 1 and 2 work well from the front with the legend open; pairs can then take one route layer each in questions 4 to 6 and report what the pop-ups say.
  • Stretch: With Measure, compare the Creole's planned voyage from Virginia to New Orleans along the sea route with the distance it sailed to Nassau, and suggest why the people on board chose Nassau.

Common misunderstandings

  • “A free state had no enslaved people.” New Jersey's pop-up says the 1850 census still counted 236 people as enslaved there.
  • “The Missouri Compromise line settled where slavery could go.” Missouri is a slave state north of the line, and in 1850 Utah and New Mexico Territories were left for their settlers to decide.
  • “People who escaped were safe once they reached a free state.” The routes on the map continue through the free states to Canada, where the cities layer marks Chatham, Toronto and Montreal.
  • “The Underground Railroad was a real railroad with fixed tracks.” The pop-up calls the routes approximate: it was a secret network of people and places, and no exact routes were recorded.

Key words

  • free state
  • slave state
  • territory
  • compromise
  • Missouri Compromise
  • Compromise of 1850
  • enslaved
  • Underground Railroad

Each state and territory is shaded in one of four groups, and a dashed line marks the Missouri Compromise line of 1820. settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History › The Civil War

Civil War Battlefields

Start with the 35 states of 1863 shaded by side, predict where the fighting happened, then turn on the battlefields and the railroads to test the prediction. Students use the pop-ups and Measure to explain why so much of the war was fought in a few places.

  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question
  • TopicThe Civil War (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.4

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Share to Google Classroom (opens in a new tab) Student sheet Teacher notes

Open in MapMaker: (opens in a new tab)

The map as it opens.

Inquiry

Compelling question

By 1863 the United States had split in two. Where was the Civil War fought, and why there?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Two blues, two oranges About 8 minutes

    With only the states layer on, students read the legend, sort the states into its four groups and use pop-ups to find when the first and last states seceded.

    From the front

    1. Open The United States in 1863 bookmark and the legend.
    2. Ask: what do the two blues have in common, and the two oranges?
    3. Click South Carolina, then Tennessee, and read the date in each pop-up.
    4. Ask: which light blue states touch an orange state?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. Before the dots About 5 minutes

    Students predict where most battles were fought and write the prediction down before the battlefield layer goes on.

    From the front

    1. Stay on The United States in 1863 bookmark with only the states layer on.
    2. Ask: if you had to shade the part of this map where most of the fighting happened, where would you shade?
    3. Have students write a prediction and a reason before anyone opens Map layers.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Turn on the battlefields If you only do one About 10 minutes

    Students turn on the battlefield layer, test their prediction, and use pop-ups to find the few battlefields in Union free states.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on Civil War battlefields.
    2. Ask: was your prediction right? Which color has most of the dots?
    3. Ask: which single state has the most?
    4. Zoom to southern Pennsylvania and click the largest dark shape. Read the name, the state and the acres.
    5. Ask: how many battlefields can you find in dark blue states?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  4. A hundred miles apart About 10 minutes

    Students measure the distance between the two capitals, Washington, D.C. and Richmond, and use it to explain the crowd of battlefields in northern Virginia.

    From the front

    1. Open the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark with the battlefields on.
    2. Find Washington and Richmond. Washington was the capital of the United States; Richmond was the capital of the Confederacy.
    3. Use Measure to draw a line from Washington to Richmond.
    4. Ask: what do you notice about the battlefields near that line?
    5. Click Maryland and Virginia and compare their groups.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Measure, how-to video: Measure with MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  5. Follow the rails About 8 minutes

    Students turn on the railroads at the same bookmark, compare the networks north and south, and check whether battlefields sit on rail lines.

    From the front

    1. Stay on the Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania bookmark and turn on Railroads in operation by 1863.
    2. Ask: where are the purple lines closest together, in the blue states or the orange states?
    3. Find First Manassas, west of Washington, and Petersburg, south of Richmond.
    4. Ask: what do those two battlefields have in common when the railroads are on?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  6. Down the Mississippi About 7 minutes

    Students move to the Mississippi Valley, find the string of battlefields along the river and work out what control of the river would do to the Confederacy.

    From the front

    1. Open The Mississippi Valley bookmark with the battlefields on. Railroads can go off to make the river easier to see.
    2. Trace the Mississippi River from Missouri down to the Gulf of Mexico.
    3. Click three battlefields that touch the river and read their names.
    4. Ask: which orange states are west of the river? What happens to them if the Union holds all of it?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  7. What the dots leave out About 6 minutes

    Students find battlefields outside the shaded states and decide what the layer can and cannot tell them.

    From the front

    1. Go back to The United States in 1863 bookmark with the battlefields on.
    2. Ask: can you find dots that are not on any shaded state?
    3. Click one and read the whole pop-up, including the last sentence.
    4. Ask: what would you want to know about this battle that the pop-up does not say?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from all three layers and at least one measurement or pop-up, then write one "why" question the map raised. Accept answers that say most battles were fought in the states that seceded and the border states, above all Virginia; that the ground between Washington and Richmond, railroad junctions and the Mississippi River drew the armies; and that few battles reached the Union free states.

Download Word (English)
