pages.summary: Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History › The early republic

The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

Find where the War of 1812 was fought, see what Spain gave up in 1819, and compare Latin America's new nations with the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicThe early republic (also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.1.6-8
    • TX 8.5(E)
    • TX 8.5(F)
    • FL SS.8.A.4.1

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Share to Google Classroom (opens in a new tab) Student sheet Teacher notes

Open in MapMaker: (opens in a new tab)

The map as it opens.

Inquiry

Compelling question

How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Where was the war fought? About 10 minutes

    Open The War of 1812 bookmark and use the battle diamonds to find the three main areas of fighting.

    From the front

    1. Open The War of 1812 bookmark.
    2. Open the legend: blue for an American victory, red for British, gray if inconclusive, and bigger diamonds for more casualties.
    3. Click a diamond near the Great Lakes and read the battle's name and dates in the pop-up.
    4. Click a diamond in each of the other clusters and use the coastline and the pop-up's account to say where it was fought.
    5. Ask: in which three areas was most of the fighting?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. The biggest battles If you only do one About 15 minutes

    Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.

    From the front

    1. Open The War of 1812 bookmark.
    2. Click the biggest diamond and read the dates under the title, the victor line and Total Casualties in the pop-up.
    3. Zoom in on the Niagara River, click the next two biggest diamonds and read the same three things.
    4. Ask: where and when was each battle fought, and who won?
    5. Write on the board: Treaty of Ghent signed December 24, 1814.
    6. Ask: which big battle came after the treaty was signed?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Zoom, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Florida and a new border About 12 minutes

    Open The 1819 boundary bookmark, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and the Adams–Onís Treaty line, and read their pop-ups to describe what the treaty settled.

    From the front

    1. Open The 1819 boundary bookmark.
    2. In Map layers, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819.
    3. Drag the map east until all of Florida shows, click the green land and read the Notes in the pop-up.
    4. Ask: what did the United States gain from Spain?
    5. Click part 1 of the pink dashed line and read its description, then click the next parts going west.
    6. Ask: where does the border follow rivers, where straight lines, and why might it switch?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine About 12 minutes

    Open Latin America in 1825, turn on the independence layer, and compare the dates of independence and US recognition with President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.

    From the front

    1. Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark.
    2. In Map layers, turn on Latin American independence and US recognition.
    3. Open the legend: blue circles recognized by 1824, orange diamonds recognized later.
    4. Click a blue circle and read the US recognition date in the pop-up.
    5. Write on the board: Monroe's message, December 2, 1823.
    6. Ask: which nations had the United States recognized before that date, and why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch of the three war fronts and of the 1819 border and the area the Monroe Doctrine covered (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. Accept answers that use the battles to show the war ended without gains, the 1819 layers to show the United States growing and fixing its border with Spain, and the independence layer to show the new nations the Monroe Doctrine spoke for.

Tools: Sketch, how-to video: Sketch on a Map (opens in a new tab)

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
C3 D2.His.1.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Analyze connections among events and developments in broader historical contexts.
TX 8.5(E)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Explain the causes, important events, and effects of the War of 1812
TX 8.5(F)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Identify the foreign policies of presidents Washington through Monroe and explain the impact of Washington's Farewell Address and the Monroe Doctrine
FL SS.8.A.4.1Framework: FloridaStandard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness (War of 1812, Convention of 1818, Adams-Onis Treaty, Missouri Compromise, Monroe Doctrine, Trail of Tears, Texas annexation, Manifest Destiny, Oregon Territory, Mexican American War/Mexican Cession, California Gold Rush, Compromise of 1850, Kansas Nebraska Act, Gadsden Purchase).

National frameworks first, then state examples. For your own state's standards, ask Vera or use the prompt under Make your own questions.

Student activity

This is what students see on the Word sheet. To edit it, download it and upload it to Google Drive (it opens in Google Docs) or open it in Word. Students need no account or login.

Download Word (English) Download Word (Español)

The Share to Google Classroom button at the top of the page shares the MapMaker map with a class, not the sheet. To assign the sheet, attach your Drive copy in Classroom and choose Make a copy for each student.

The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?

Open the map in MapMaker: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

Before you start

In the early 1800s Britain and France were at war, and both seized American ships. British warships also forced sailors off American ships into the Royal Navy, and Britain supported Native nations resisting American settlement. In June 1812 the United States declared war on Britain.

Reading the map

The map has no place names: click a feature to see its name. Pink shading shows the United States in 1800. Diamonds mark battles; use the legend: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if neither side won; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. The legend says British for every opponent, but some battles were fought against Native nations: the pop-up's story tells you who fought. Each battle pop-up gives the dates, the victor and the casualties. Tan shading shows battlefield land when you zoom in close to a battle. Three layers are off when the map opens: the land Spain gave up in 1819 (green), the treaty line (pink dashes, in seven parts) and the Latin American nations, shown as blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824 and orange diamonds if later; the pop-up gives the exact date.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Where was the war fought?

    On the map:

    1. Open The War of 1812 bookmark.
    2. Click some diamonds in each group and read their pop-ups.

    Answer: In which three areas was most of the fighting?

  2. The biggest battles

    On the map:

    1. Click the three biggest diamonds. Zoom in on the Niagara River, between Lake Erie and Lake Ontario, where several large diamonds sit close together.
    2. Read when each battle was fought and who won. Work out where from the map and the pop-up's account.
    3. Compare each battle's date with December 24, 1814, when the peace treaty was signed at Ghent.

    Answer: Where and when was each battle fought, and who won? Which big battle came after the peace treaty?

  3. Florida and a new border

    On the map:

    1. Open The 1819 boundary bookmark.
    2. In Map layers, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819.
    3. Click the green land and read its pop-up. Drag the map east to see all of Florida.
    4. Click each part of the pink dashed line and read its pop-up.

    Answer: What did the United States gain from Spain? Where does the new border follow rivers, and where does it follow straight lines? Why might a border switch from one to the other?

  4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine

    On the map:

    1. Open the Latin America in 1825 bookmark.
    2. Turn on Latin American independence and US recognition.
    3. Click the blue circles and read each recognition date in the pop-up.
    4. Check each date against December 2, 1823 (blue only means recognized by 1824).

    Answer: Which nations had the United States recognized before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823? Why might Monroe have warned European powers to stay out of the Americas?

Your answer: Answer the big question. Compare the country at the end of the war with the country in 1823, using one battle and one later layer.

Looking back

The war itself changed no borders. Which layer on this map shows the biggest change, and what caused it?

Español: Spanish draft for review by a native speaker. Layer and bookmark names stay in English, as they appear in MapMaker.

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography, Government. Grade: 8. Time: About 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Use the battle diamonds in the Battles of the War of 1812 layer to identify the three main areas of fighting.
  • Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.
  • Read the pop-ups of the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line layers to describe what the treaty settled.
  • Compare the dates of independence and US recognition in the Latin American independence layer with Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.
  • Use the locations of the battles and the 1819 boundary as evidence to explain how the United States' position in North America changed between 1812 and 1823.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Reading pop-ups
  • Using a map legend
  • Navigating a map
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Sketching on a map

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: When the map opens, the boundaries and battles are on and three layers are off: Land Spain gave up in 1819, Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819, and Latin American independence and US recognition. Students turn them on for questions 3 and 4.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. The battle diamonds cluster in three areas far apart. From the map, what was each side trying to control in each area, and why was none of them decisive?
  2. The Battle of New Orleans was fought after the Treaty of Ghent was signed. Looking at where Ghent and New Orleans are, what does that gap tell you about how news traveled and how wars ended in 1815?
  3. Most Latin American nations had declared independence before Monroe's 1823 message, and the United States recognized several of them. Comparing the dates on the map, was the Monroe Doctrine leading events or following them?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do question 2 from the front, reading the dates, the victor line and Total Casualties aloud, and keep the legend open on the board with the Treaty of Ghent date.
  • Stretch: Click the diamonds at Tippecanoe, Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend, read in each account who fought, and explain why the legend's British label does not fit.

Common misunderstandings

  • “The United States won the War of 1812 and gained land.” The Treaty of Ghent returned the borders to where they were before the war, and the map shows American and British victories on every front.
  • “The Battle of New Orleans won the war.” It was fought on January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814.
  • “Every battle was against British soldiers.” The battles in Alabama were part of the Creek War, fought against the Red Stick Creeks.
  • “Every blue circle was recognized before the Monroe Doctrine.” Blue means recognized by the end of 1824. Brazil and the Federation of Central America were recognized in 1824, after Monroe's message of December 2, 1823; the pop-up dates show it.

Key words

  • impressment
  • blockade
  • Treaty of Ghent
  • cession
  • boundary
  • recognition
  • Monroe Doctrine
  • independence

Further reading

  • War of 1812 (opens in a new tab) (National Park Service)
  • Treaty of Ghent (1814) (opens in a new tab) (National Archives)
  • Monroe Doctrine (1823) (opens in a new tab) (National Archives)

Answers

Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept are kept off this page, so it can be shared with students: answer notes (web page) or Download Word (teacher notes). The answer page also has a rubric for the answer to the compelling question and a model answer.

About this map

This map spans North and South America. It shows national borders in 1800, with the United States shaded pink, and 52 battles from 1811 to 1815, most from the War of 1812 itself, with battlefield land that appears when you zoom in close. Three layers, off when the map opens, add the land Spain gave up in 1819, the Adams–Onís Treaty line, and ten Latin American nations labeled with the year each became independent, with symbols showing whether the United States recognized them by 1824 or later.

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Historic National Boundaries: 1800What it shows: Borders in 1800, before the Louisiana Purchase, with the United States shaded pink. Each pop-up names the country.Source: University of Minnesota (historic national boundaries), from the MapMaker catalogue
Land Spain gave up in 1819 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Land Spain gave up in the Adams–Onís Treaty, including East and West Florida (green). Each pop-up gives a short note.Source: MapMaker catalogue (US territorial acquisitions)
Battlefield Boundaries: War of 1812What it shows: The land each battlefield covered (tan) and its core area (lighter tan). It draws only when zoomed in close to a battle. Each pop-up gives the battle and its size in acres.Source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program
Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 (off when the map opens)What it shows: The 1819 boundary with Spain as a pink dashed line in seven parts, drawn from the treaty's description and approximate. Each pop-up describes its part.Source: Treaty text from the Avalon Project, Yale Law School; drawn on Natural Earth rivers
Battles of the War of 1812What it shows: 52 battles from 1811 to 1815 as diamonds: blue for an American victory, red for a British victory, gray if inconclusive; bigger diamonds mean more casualties. Each pop-up gives the dates, the victor, total casualties, a short account and a casualties chart; it does not show the state or the leaders. The legend labels every opponent of the United States as British, but some battles were fought against Native nations: Tippecanoe (the Shawnee-led confederacy), Fort Mims and Horseshoe Bend (Red Stick Creeks). The pop-up's account says who fought.Source: American Battlefield Trust (War of 1812 Battles map)
Latin American independence and US recognition (off when the map opens)What it shows: Ten Latin American nations, labeled with the year of independence: blue circles if the United States recognized them by 1824, orange diamonds if it recognized them later (1826 to 1862). Each pop-up gives the capital, today's countries, independence and recognition.Source: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State; Library of Congress country studies

Bookmarks: The War of 1812; The 1819 boundary; Latin America in 1825.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › US History › Age of Jackson

Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894

Turn on one period at a time to watch American Indian land cessions spread across the United States, predict where the next ones will be, and explain why the 1830s cessions are where they are. The map is Charles Royce's record of cessions, so students also ask whose view it shows.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer the compelling question with evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised for them. The students' own questions are a good place to start the next lesson, for example on the Trail of Tears.

Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: How did the United States gain American Indian land between 1784 and 1894, and why did the pattern change in the 1830s?

Open the map in MapMaker: Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894

Before you start

A treaty is a written agreement between nations. A cession is land a nation gives up, usually in a treaty. On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. It let the President make treaties to move American Indian nations from east of the Mississippi River to land in the West. In December 1830, Jackson told Congress that removal meant "opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites." The map comes from records Charles Royce made from government documents. The government published them in 1899.

Reading the map

Light blue: cessions dated before 1830. Orange: 1830 to 1839. Green: 1840 to 1894. Only light blue is on at the start; turn on the others in Map layers when a question asks. Where layers overlap, the colors mix: click the area to read its dates. Some areas have two or more dates. The first date can be a treaty that kept the land for the nation, so read every date. Click an area to open its pop-up; scroll to see all of it.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Notice: before 1830

    On the map:

    1. Open The United States bookmark.
    2. Find the light blue areas (Cessions dated before 1830) in the legend and on the map.
    3. Open The Southeast bookmark and look for gaps: places in Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia with no light blue.

    Answer: (a) Name three states where the United States gained land before 1830. (b) Name one big part of the United States with no light blue. (c) Which Southeast states have gaps with no light blue?

  2. Predict

    On the map:

    1. Keep only Cessions dated before 1830 on.
    2. Look at the gaps you found in the Southeast, and at the empty parts east and west of the Mississippi River (the long river that runs down the middle of the country to the Gulf of Mexico).
    3. Write your prediction before you turn on any other layer.

    Answer: Where do you expect the cessions of the 1830s to be? Why there? I predict the 1830s cessions will be in because .

  3. Reveal: the 1830s

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (orange).
    2. Open The Southeast bookmark, then The Old Northwest bookmark (the Great Lakes states).
    3. Compare the orange areas (Cessions dated 1830 to 1839) with your prediction.

    Answer: (a) Name three states with orange areas (Cessions dated 1830 to 1839). (b) Was your prediction right? (c) What happened to the gaps you found in the Southeast in question 1?

  4. Explain why

    On the map:

    1. Make sure Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 (orange) is on, and open The Southeast bookmark.
    2. Click three orange areas: in Mississippi north-east of Jackson; in Alabama north of Montgomery, near the Georgia line; in the north-west corner of Georgia.
    3. For each one, write the nation (the title of the pop-up), the date, and the words on the first link (for example Treaty text). You don't need to open the link.

    Answer: (a) Fill in the nation, date and link words for each area. (b) In December 1830 Jackson told Congress that removal meant "opening the whole territory between Tennessee on the north and Louisiana on the south to the settlement of the whites." Using his words and the Indian Removal Act (Before you start), why might these cessions have come in the 1830s, and why here? Mississippi: , , Alabama: , , Georgia: , ,

  5. Reveal: 1840 to 1894

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 (green).
    2. Open The United States bookmark, then The Plains and the West bookmark.

    Answer: (a) Where are most of the green areas (Cessions dated 1840 to 1894)? (b) Name one part of the United States with no cessions at all on this map.

  6. Question the source

    On the map:

    1. Click the orange area in the north-west corner of Georgia (Cherokee). Scroll to the end of the pop-up and read the last sentence.
    2. Click the orange area in Alabama north of Montgomery (Creek) and read Nations today.

    Answer: (a) Who recorded these cessions, and from whose records? (b) What is missing from the Creek pop-up? (c) In 1836, 3,352 Cherokees signed a petition saying the treaty was made "without any authority from the council or people of the Nation." How does that change how you read the Cherokee pop-up?

Your answer: Answer the big question, How did the United States gain American Indian land between 1784 and 1894, and why did the pattern change in the 1830s?, using evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups. Then write one "why" question this map raises for you.

Looking back

Turning the layers on one at a time, what did you notice about how the cessions spread that you might have missed on a finished map?

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Geography. Grade: 8. Time: About 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Describe where the United States had gained American Indian land before 1830, using the Cessions dated before 1830 layer and the legend.
  • Make a prediction about the next period from the map, then turn on the 1830s layer and test it.
  • Read the nation, date and kind of document in the pop-ups of three 1830s cessions in the Southeast.
  • Explain the 1830s pattern in the Southeast using the Indian Removal Act (1830) as evidence.
  • Evaluate the map as a source: who recorded the cessions, when, and whose view is missing.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Using a map legend
  • Turning map layers on and off
  • Reading pop-ups

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: The map opens with only Cessions dated before 1830 on. Students turn on the 1830s layer in question 3 and the 1840 to 1894 layer in question 5; question 2's prediction works best before the later layers are on. State names, cities and rivers are labeled above the colored areas, and the steps use them to say where to click (for example, north-east of Jackson). The sheet names each layer by its date as well as its color.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. Your prediction in question 2: what did you base it on, and what did the 1830s layer show that you didn't expect?
  2. The map shows where and when, but not why. What other evidence would you need to explain a single cession, such as the Cherokee cession of 1835?
  3. Royce called these areas cessions. Is cession a fair word for all of them? What other words might the nations named in the pop-ups use?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do questions 1 and 3 from the front with the legend open, and point out the three places to click in question 4 (north-east of Jackson, north of Montgomery, the north-west corner of Georgia) on the projected map.
  • Stretch: Open the Treaty text link for the Cherokee cession of 1835 and find one article about moving west; compare it with what the pop-up and Before you start say.

Common misunderstandings

  • “Empty parts of the map, such as New England and Virginia, were never American Indian land.” Royce's record starts in 1784. Land taken in colonial times, or by the states, isn't on this map.
  • “Two dates in a pop-up mean the land was ceded twice.” Royce lists every treaty that concerns an area. In central Florida, the 1823 treaty set the land aside as a Seminole reservation and the 1832 treaty ceded it.
  • “A cession means a nation chose to sell its land.” Many cessions were made under pressure or disputed; the map is the federal government's record of them, as the pop-up note says.
  • “A bigger colored area means more land was taken in that period.” The same land can appear in more than one layer: most of Oklahoma is light blue, orange and green, because Royce lists every treaty that concerns an area. The basemap's projection also makes northern areas look larger than southern ones.

  • treaty
  • cession
  • Indian Removal Act

  • petition

About this map

This map shows the land the United States gained from American Indian nations by treaty, act of Congress or executive order between 1784 and 1894, from the records Charles Royce compiled for the federal government (published 1899). There is one layer for each period: before 1830, the 1830s and 1840 to 1894. Only the cessions dated before 1830 are on when the map opens; students turn on the later periods themselves. State names, cities and rivers are labeled above the colored areas. Each area's pop-up gives the nation named in the record, the date or dates, today's states and the nations that exist today, and most link to the treaty, statute or executive order.

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

See how each state's electors voted in 1828, then turn on who could vote there: the property and tax rules for white men, and whether free Black men could vote. Students test the idea that Jackson's election was a victory for the common man against the rules state by state.

The map as it opens.

Inquiry

Compelling question

Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 is often called a victory for the common man. Who could vote in 1828, and did it depend on where you lived?

Pick the questions that suit your class: each one is answered from the map and says about how long it takes. The one marked If you only do one gets to the big question on its own in about 15 minutes. Under each question, From the front gives the exact clicks for teaching it on a projector. Answers and what to accept are linked under Teacher notes.

  1. Notice: the result About 8 minutes

    With only the votes layer on, find which states voted for Jackson and which for Adams, and the states that split.

    From the front

    1. Open The 24 states of 1828 bookmark.
    2. Open the legend: blue is Andrew Jackson, orange is John Quincy Adams, and bigger pies mean more electors.
    3. Ask: which part of the country voted mostly for Adams, and which for Jackson?
    4. Click the pie on New York and read the votes.
    5. Ask: which states split their electors between the two?

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  2. Predict About 5 minutes

    Before turning on the voting-rule layers, students predict where white men had to own property or pay a tax to vote, and where free Black men could vote, with a reason. They write the prediction down first.

    From the front

    1. Keep only Election of 1828: electors' votes on.
    2. Ask: in which states do you think white men still had to own property or pay a tax to vote? Older states on the coast, or newer states in the West?
    3. Ask: where do you think free Black men could vote? Have students write their predictions before anyone turns on a layer.

    Tools: Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  3. Reveal: white men About 8 minutes

    Turn on White men and the vote, 1828 and compare the shading with the prediction and with the votes.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn on White men and the vote, 1828.
    2. Scroll down the legend to the key: light green is no property or tax rule, middle green is pay a tax (or a similar rule), dark green is own property.
    3. Ask: which two states are dark? Open the New England and New York bookmark to find Rhode Island.
    4. Ask: where are the light states, and did Jackson win only in states with no rule?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  4. Reveal: free Black men If you only do one About 15 minutes

    Turn off the white men layer and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828; compare with question 3.

    From the front

    1. In Map layers, turn off White men and the vote, 1828 and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828.
    2. Scroll down the legend to the key: light green is could vote, middle green is only with extra rules or kept out in practice, dark green is could not vote.
    3. Ask: in which states could free Black men vote on the same terms as white men?
    4. Open the New England and New York bookmark and click New York. Read White men and Free Black men.
    5. Ask: Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri had no property or tax rule for white men. What does this layer show for free Black men there?

    Tools: Map layers, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Legend, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab) · Bookmarks, how-to video: Navigating MapMaker (opens in a new tab)

  5. Explain why About 8 minutes

    Read the pop-ups for South Carolina and Delaware (the legislature chose electors) and Georgia (voters chose them for the first time); explain what that meant for who could vote for president.

    From the front

    1. Click South Carolina and read Who chose the electors. Then open The Middle Atlantic bookmark and click Delaware.
    2. Ask: did voters in these states choose the president's electors?
    3. Click Georgia and read Who chose the electors.
    4. Ask: what changed in Georgia in 1828?
    5. Ask: in South Carolina and Delaware, could a man who met the voting rules vote for president?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

  6. Question the source About 6 minutes

    Students ask what the map can and can't show: it shows the rules in law, not who actually voted.

    From the front

    1. Click Pennsylvania and read Free Black men.
    2. Ask: what is the difference between what the law said and what happened?
    3. Ask: what would you need, besides this map, to know how many people actually voted in 1828?

    Tools: Pop-ups, how-to video: Explore Layers and Data (opens in a new tab)

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised. Accept answers that say who could vote depended on the state, name the property states (Virginia and Rhode Island) and the tax states, note that free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men in only six states and women in none, and weigh the 'common man' description: more white men could vote, and many people could not.

Student sheet

Name Date

Big question: Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 is often called a victory for the common man. Who could vote in 1828, and did it depend on where you lived?

Open the map in MapMaker: The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote

Before you start

In 1828, Americans did not vote for the president directly. Each state chose electors, and the electors voted for president. Andrew Jackson ran against President John Quincy Adams. Each state made its own rules about who could vote. Some states made men own land or pay a tax to vote. Suffrage means the right to vote. A legislature is a state's lawmakers. The militia was a state's citizen soldiers.

Reading the map

Blue pies: electors for Andrew Jackson. Orange pies: John Quincy Adams. Bigger pies mean more electors. Only the pies are on at the start; turn on the other layers in Map layers when a question asks. Both rule layers are green. In both, light green means fewer limits and dark green means more. The key for these layers is lower down in the legend: scroll to see it. Click a state to read its votes, its rules and the sources; scroll to see all of the pop-up.

Tip: If a pop-up says 1 of 2 (or more), more than one thing is at that spot. Use the arrows in the pop-up to see each one.

Questions

  1. Notice: the result

    On the map:

    1. Open The 24 states of 1828 bookmark and open the legend.
    2. Find the blue pies (Andrew Jackson) and the orange pies (John Quincy Adams).
    3. Click the two-color pies and read the votes in each pop-up.

    Answer: (a) Which parts of the country voted mostly for Adams, and which for Jackson? (b) Which three states split their electors?

  2. Predict

    On the map:

    1. Keep only Election of 1828: electors' votes on.
    2. Write your predictions before you turn on any other layer.

    Answer: (a) Where do you think white men still had to own property or pay a tax to vote? (b) Where do you think free Black men could vote? Give a reason for each. I predict because .

  3. Reveal: white men

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn on White men and the vote, 1828.
    2. Scroll down the legend to its key: light green means no property or tax rule, middle green means pay a tax (or a similar rule), dark green means own property.
    3. Click a dark state and a light state and read White men in each pop-up. Rhode Island is small: use the New England and New York bookmark.

    Answer: (a) Which two states are shaded dark? (b) Where are the light states (no rule)? (c) Did Jackson win only in states with no rule? Was your prediction right?

  4. Reveal: free Black men

    On the map:

    1. In Map layers, turn off White men and the vote, 1828 and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828.
    2. Scroll down the legend to its key and find the light green states (could vote).
    3. Open the New England and New York bookmark, click New York and read White men and Free Black men.

    Answer: (a) Name the states where free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men. (b) How were New York's rules for white men and for Black men different? (c) Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri had no property or tax rule for white men. What does this layer show for free Black men there?

  5. Explain why

    On the map:

    1. Click South Carolina and read Who chose the electors. Then open The Middle Atlantic bookmark and click Delaware.
    2. Click Georgia and read Who chose the electors.

    Answer: (a) Who chose the electors in South Carolina and Delaware? (b) What changed in Georgia in 1828? (c) In South Carolina and Delaware, could a man who met the voting rules vote for president? What does that add to your answer about who could vote?

  6. Question the source

    On the map:

    1. Click Pennsylvania and read Free Black men.
    2. Read the sentence about women at the end of any pop-up.

    Answer: (a) In Pennsylvania, how was what happened different from what the law said? (b) Which people does the map not show? (c) What else would you need to find out how many people actually voted in 1828?

Your answer: Answer the big question, Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 is often called a victory for the common man. Who could vote in 1828, and did it depend on where you lived?, using evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups. Then write one "why" question this map raises for you.

Looking back

Turning on the rules one layer at a time, what did you notice about who could vote that a list of election results would not show?

Teacher notes

Subjects: US History, Civics, Geography. Grade: 8. Time: About 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question.

Learning objectives

Students will:

  • Describe the result of the 1828 election by region using the pies, legend and pop-ups.
  • Make and test a prediction about where white men had to own property or pay a tax to vote.
  • Compare the rules for white men and for free Black men in the same states, including New York.
  • Explain what expanded suffrage meant in 1828 and for whom, using evidence from the pop-ups.
  • Distinguish what the law said from what happened, using Pennsylvania as an example.

Map skills

  • Using bookmarks to find places
  • Using a map legend
  • Reading pop-ups
  • Turning map layers on and off

Ways to run this lesson

  • Front-of-class demonstration
  • 1:1 devices
  • Computer lab
  • Homework or flipped classroom

Before class

About this map: The map opens with only Election of 1828: electors' votes on. Students turn on White men and the vote, 1828 in question 3 and Free Black men and the vote, 1828 in question 4; question 2's prediction works best before those layers are on. State names come from today's basemap: a few are under pies, and some named places were territories in 1828; clicking a state gives its name. Small states are easier to click with the New England and New York and The Middle Atlantic bookmarks. Jackson's supporters presented him as a champion of ordinary people, and many textbooks describe 1828 as a victory for the common man; the lesson tests that description. Virginia's pop-up quotes the 1785 law's own words, "free negroes or mulattoes", as a primary source; you may want to say so before students read it.

Materials, ways to prepare and how every lesson works are on How these lessons work.

Discussion questions

  1. Your predictions in question 2: what did you base them on, and what surprised you?
  2. New York removed the property rule for white men but kept one for Black men. Why might a state do both at once?
  3. Is 'a victory for the common man' a fair way to describe 1828? Who would agree, and who might not?

Support and stretch

  • Support: Do questions 1, 3 and 4 from the front with the legend open, and give pairs a list of the six states where free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men to check on the map.
  • Stretch: Open the source link in New York's pop-up, find the 1822 version of the voting clause, and find the words that set the $250 rule; compare them with the rule for white men.

Common misunderstandings

  • “In 1828 every white man could vote.” Virginia and Rhode Island still required property, and ten states required a tax or a similar rule (militia service, road work or a little land).
  • “Jackson won because the states with the most open rules voted for him.” The map doesn't show that: Jackson won Virginia, a property state, and Adams won states with no property or tax rule.
  • “Voters chose the electors in every state.” In South Carolina and Delaware the state legislature chose them.
  • “If the law allowed it, people could vote.” In Pennsylvania the law didn't mention race, but officials kept many Black men from voting.

Key words

  • suffrage
  • elector
  • legislature
  • militia
  • property requirement
  • the common man

Further reading

  • 1828 Electoral College Results (opens in a new tab) (National Archives)
  • New York Constitution of 1821 and the 1826 amendment (opens in a new tab) (50 Constitutions project)
  • Constitution of North Carolina, 1776 (Arts. VII and VIII) (opens in a new tab) (Avalon Project, Yale Law School)
  • Voting Rights in New Jersey before the 15th and 19th Amendments (opens in a new tab) (National Park Service)

Answers

Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept are kept off this page, so it can be shared with students: answer notes (web page) or Download Word (teacher notes). The answer page also has a rubric for the answer to the compelling question and a model answer.

About this map

This map shows the presidential election of 1828 in the 24 states of that year. A pie on each state shows how its electors voted, for Andrew Jackson or John Quincy Adams, with bigger pies for more electors. Two layers, off when the map opens, show who could vote in each state: whether white men had to own property or pay a tax, and whether free Black men could vote. Each state's pop-up gives the votes, how its electors were chosen, the rules and their sources.

Each layer names its source, so you can check where the information comes from.

LayerWhat it showsSource
Election of 1828: electors' votesWhat it shows: A pie on each of the 24 states: electors' votes for Andrew Jackson (blue) and John Quincy Adams (orange), with bigger pies for more electors. The pop-up gives the votes, who chose the electors and both voting rules, with sources.Source: National Archives (Electoral College results, 1828); state outlines from Natural Earth
Free Black men and the vote, 1828 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Each state shaded green by whether free Black men could vote: light green, could vote on the same terms as white men; middle green, only with extra rules or kept out in practice; dark green, could not vote. Off when the map opens.Source: State constitutions and laws, as cited in each pop-up
White men and the vote, 1828 (off when the map opens)What it shows: Each state shaded green by its rule for white men: light green, no property or tax rule; middle green, had to pay a tax or meet a similar rule (militia service, road work or a little land); dark green, had to own property. Off when the map opens.Source: State constitutions and laws, as cited in each pop-up

Bookmarks: The 24 states of 1828; New England and New York; The Middle Atlantic.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

Answer notes: 1775–1776 Revolutionary Battles

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 62 minutes: 52 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicRoad to revolution and the Revolution
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • TX 8.4(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.6

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Why did the fighting move from Boston to New York, and then across New Jersey, in 1775–1776?

1. Where did the war begin?

Open the Massachusetts bookmark and click the Lexington and Concord diamond, then the Boston diamond. Read the dates in each pop-up, and the winner from the diamond's color and the legend. Measure the straight-line distance from Boston to Concord.

Where to find it on the mapMassachusetts bookmark. Lexington and Concord pop-up, the date line under the title: April 19, 1775. Legend (Revolutionary War Battles): blue diamond = American Victory, red = British Victory. Boston pop-up: April 19, 1775 to March 17, 1776, about 11 months. Measure tool, from the Boston diamond to the Lexington and Concord diamond: about 17 miles (accept 15 to 18). The Lexington and Concord pop-up's account says Concord is 20 miles northwest of Boston; accept that if a student quotes it.

Accept answers thatThe date, the winner and about 11 months, and the point that the war began about 17 miles from Boston, a short march from the British army's base.

NotesUse the Revolutionary War Battles legend for the result.

2. Where was the fighting in 1775, and where in 1776?

Zoom out one step from the Massachusetts bookmark and drag the map from Quebec to South Carolina to find all 21 diamonds (they disappear if you zoom out too far). Click each one, read its dates, and sort the battles into two lists by year. Use the legend for the winner. Which colonies saw fighting each year, and what changed?

Where to find it on the mapRevolutionary War Battles layer, one zoom step out from the Massachusetts bookmark and dragged along the coast: 21 diamonds. Each pop-up's date line gives the year; the diamond color and the legend give the winner. The colony comes from the names printed on the map by the Thirteen British Colonies layer, or from the pop-up's account; Quebec is not labeled.

Accept answers thatNames Massachusetts, New York and Virginia, and Quebec (a British province, not one of the thirteen colonies), for 1775 and adds North Carolina, South Carolina, New Jersey and Rhode Island for 1776, and says that the fighting began around Boston and then spread along the coast, with most battles from August 1776 in New York and New Jersey, where the British won nearly all of them.

Answer key
YearAmerican victoriesBritish victories
1775 (8 battles)American victories: Lexington and Concord, Boston (siege) and Gloucester (Massachusetts); Fort Ticonderoga and Crown Point (New York); Great Bridge (Virginia)British victories: Bunker Hill (Massachusetts); Quebec (Quebec)
1776 (13 battles)American victories: Moores Creek Bridge (North Carolina); Sullivan's Island and Breach Inlet (South Carolina); Gwynn's Island (Virginia); Trenton (New Jersey)British victories: Brooklyn, Valcour Island, Pell's Point, White Plains, Fort Washington (New York); Fort Lee, Mount Holly (New Jersey); Newport (Rhode Island)

NotesClicking a colony opens nothing, and clicking a colony border opens a list of data fields (FID, LEFT_FID and others) that no question uses.

3. Why New York?

Turn on Key Port Cities in Map layers. Students use the legend to tell a Major Port City from a smaller Port, click the major ports between Boston and Charleston to read their names, measure New York to Philadelphia and New York to Boston, and say what a navy based at New York could reach.

Where to find it on the mapKey Port Cities layer, legend: larger symbol = Major Port City, smaller = Port. Five major ports: Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Norfolk and Charleston, so the three between Boston and Charleston are New York, Philadelphia and Norfolk. The layer has no labels, but each port's pop-up gives its name in bold (for example New York, NY and Norfolk, VA). Measure tool: New York to Philadelphia about 80 miles (accept 75 to 85); New York to Boston about 190 miles (accept 180 to 200).

Accept answers thatNames at least New York and Philadelphia, gives both distances within range, and uses the map to say that New York is a major port in the middle of the coast, about 80 miles from Philadelphia and 190 from Boston by Measure, so a navy based there could reach the other big ports and cut New England off from the colonies to the south.

NotesBackground for teachers: Battle of Brooklyn, American Battlefield Trust (opens in a new tab).

4. How did 1776 end?

Zoom in near New York City until the numbered turning points show, and follow circles 4 and 5. Click the diamonds for Fort Washington, Fort Lee and Trenton, and read the dates and the winner from the legend. Measure the distance from the Brooklyn diamond (New York City) to Trenton.

Where to find it on the mapTurning Points circles 4 (Fall of New York City, 1776, Victor: Britain) and 5 (Washington Strikes Back, 1776, Victor: United States); the pop-up's Battle details text tells the story of each. Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups: Fort Washington, November 16, 1776, and Fort Lee, November 20, 1776, red = British Victory; Trenton, December 26, 1776, blue = American Victory. Measure tool, from the Brooklyn diamond (New York City) to Trenton: about 52 miles (accept 48 to 56). From the Fort Washington or Fort Lee diamonds it is about 61 miles; accept that if a student measured from there. Circles 4 and 5 sit on the Fort Washington and Trenton diamonds, so a click opens the circle first and the battle is the second pop-up.

Accept answers thatThe three dates and winners, and about 52 miles: by December 26, 1776 the fighting had moved across New Jersey to Trenton.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a route drawn with Sketch (not saved, so finish in one session or take a screenshot), or a short talk using the bookmark and the layers.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use dates and victors from the Revolutionary War Battles pop-ups and legend (Lexington and Concord, April 19, 1775, blue = American Victory; Fort Washington, November 16, 1776, red = British Victory; Trenton, December 26, 1776), the Major Port City symbol in the Key Port Cities legend, the Turning Points circles, and a Measure distance such as New York to Boston (about 190 miles).

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The fighting moved because the British gave up Boston and went after New York, the big port in the middle of the coast. The war began close to Boston: Lexington and Concord was fought on April 19, 1775, about 16 miles from the city, and the Americans won. The siege of Boston lasted about 11 months, until March 17, 1776. After that most battles were around New York. New York is a major port about 190 miles from Boston and 80 miles from Philadelphia, so a navy there could reach the other big ports and cut New England off from the colonies to the south. The British won at Brooklyn, Fort Washington and Fort Lee, and Washington's army fell back across New Jersey. On December 26, 1776, about 52 miles from New York City, the Americans won at Trenton.

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.10(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
TX 8.4(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Explain the issues surrounding important events of the American Revolution, including declaring independence; fighting the battles of Lexington and Concord, Saratoga, and Yorktown; enduring the winter at Valley Forge; and signing the Treaty of Paris of 1783 (partial: this lesson covers the opening phase of the Revolution, 1775–1776).
FL SS.8.A.3.6Framework: FloridaStandard: Examine the causes, course, and consequences of the American Revolution

National frameworks first, then state examples. For your own state's standards, ask Vera or use the prompt under Make your own questions.

pages.title: Answer notes: Roads, Trails, and Rails West
pages.summary: Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept, for the MapMaker lesson Roads, Trails, and Rails West. For teachers.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › Roads, Trails, and Rails West

Answer notes: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicWestward expansion and Manifest Destiny (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.7.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.11(A)
    • TX 8.6(B)
    • TX 8.6(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.4.1

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?

1. Where did the trails begin?

Click three trails (use the legend to tell them apart) and note from each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?

Where to find it on the mapTrails West pop-ups (title is the trail name, the text gives the places). Most trails start in Missouri: Independence (Oregon, California), St. Joseph (Pony Express), St. Louis (Butterfield Overland) or Missouri in general (Santa Fe). On the map, the Mormon Pioneer trail's eastern end is at Nauvoo, Illinois, on the Mississippi, and its pop-up mentions Nauvoo and Omaha.

Accept answers thatMissouri. For why, a good answer uses the map: Missouri was at the western edge of the settled states and on the Missouri River, so it was the last place to buy supplies and the river was the way in.

Answer key
TrailFromTo
OregonFrom: Independence, MissouriTo: Willamette River valley, near Portland, Oregon
CaliforniaFrom: Independence, Missouri, and Omaha, NebraskaTo: Northern California
Mormon PioneerFrom: Nauvoo, Illinois (the line's eastern end on the map), then past Omaha, NebraskaTo: Salt Lake City, Utah
Santa FeFrom: MissouriTo: Santa Fe, New Mexico
Pony ExpressFrom: St. Joseph, MissouriTo: Sacramento, California
Butterfield OverlandFrom: St. Louis, Missouri, and Memphis, Tennessee, via Fort Smith, ArkansasTo: San Francisco, California
Old SpanishFrom: Abiquiú, New MexicoTo: Los Angeles, California

2. How far, and how many?

Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri (on the basemap, just east of Kansas City), to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.

Where to find it on the mapOregon Trail pop-up: about 2,000 miles (3,219 km); 300,000 to 400,000 people between 1840 and 1860. Measure tool, Independence to Portland: about 1,500 miles (accept 1,450 to 1,550).

Accept answers thatThe trail is about 500 miles longer than the straight line. Says the dotted line bends to follow rivers (the pop-up names the Platte, North Platte, Snake and Columbia) for water and grass, and crosses the mountains through passes rather than straight over them.

3. Whose land?

Turn on Indigenous Territories in Map layers and zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail from end to end. Was the West empty land when the trails were built? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

Where to find it on the mapIndigenous Territories layer (off at start; names draw when zoomed in, and a click on the shading opens a pop-up with the nation's name). Any trail runs through a continuous patchwork of shaded territories from Missouri to the coast; for example the Oregon Trail crosses lands labeled Kaw / Kansa, Pawnee, Očhéthi Šakówiŋ (the Sioux nations, including the Lakota), Cheyenne, Arapaho, Eastern Shoshone, Shoshone-Bannock, and Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla. Accept any two names read from the map.

Accept answers thatNo, the land was not empty: the layer shows nations' territories along the whole trail. For the second part, a good answer reasons from the map that hundreds of thousands of travelers, their wagons and animals crossed these lands, so it could mean lost hunting grounds and grass, disease, pressure on water, forts and settlements along the route, and later loss of the land itself; any reasoned effect, positive or negative, that connects the trail to the people living there is acceptable.

4. From trails to rails

Turn on the Railroads group in Map layers. Using the legend, which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line near a trail, read when it was in operation, and compare the year with 1869, when the California Trail stopped being used (the thick transcontinental lines have no pop-up).

Where to find it on the mapLegend: Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) are thick colored lines running from Omaha across Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada to Sacramento. Compare with the dotted California and Mormon Pioneer trails (and the Pony Express across Nevada). Railroads 1826 to 1911 pop-up: "Railroad in operation by:" followed by a year. West of the Missouri River the layer's earliest lines are dated 1865 (Nebraska), 1867 (Wyoming), 1868 (Nevada) and 1869 (Utah); California and Texas have lines from the 1850s. The California Trail pop-up says the trail was used until 1869, when the transcontinental railroad was completed.

Accept answers thatThe California and Mormon Pioneer trails (also the Pony Express across Nevada). A year read from a gray line's pop-up, correctly placed before or after 1869. Most lines along the trails west of the Missouri River date from the late 1860s or later, so the railroads arrived as the wagon trails went out of use, and ran along the same river valleys and passes.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, one journey sketched on the map with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the Trails West pop-ups (the Oregon Trail's about 2,000 miles and 300,000 to 400,000 people, 1840 to 1860; the California Trail used until 1869), Measure from Independence to Portland (about 1,500 miles), nations named on the Indigenous Territories layer, and the legend's Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines beside the dotted trails.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).

A model answer (level 4)

The trails and railroads opened the West to settlers, but they ran through land where Indigenous nations already lived. The Oregon Trail pop-up says the trail was about 2,000 miles long and that 300,000 to 400,000 people traveled it between 1840 and 1860. A straight line from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon, is only about 1,500 miles, because the trail bends to follow rivers like the Platte and the Snake. When I turned on Indigenous Territories, the trail crossed the lands of the Pawnee, Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, Cheyenne and Shoshone, so the land was not empty. All those wagons and animals used up grass and hunting grounds. Later the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroad ran close to the California and Mormon Pioneer trails. The California Trail was used until 1869, when the railroad was finished. For settlers the trip got faster. For the nations, more people kept coming.

Lessons › US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850

Answer notes: US Slavery and the Slave Trade, 1850

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question
  • TopicReform and the road to war (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.2

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

By 1850, how did slavery divide the United States, and what did that division mean for the people who were enslaved?

1. Four groups

With only the opening layers on, students read the legend, place a few states and territories in their groups, and find what New Jersey's pop-up adds to the word free.

Where to find it on the mapFree and slave states and territories, 1850 layer, legend and pop-ups. California: Free state (a state from 1850). Texas: Slave state (and Washington, D.C.) (a state from 1845); students can write slave state. Oregon Territory: Free territory. New Mexico Territory: Territory open to slavery. New Jersey: "An 1846 law abolished slavery here but kept the last enslaved people bound to their owners as 'apprentices'. The 1850 census still counted 236 people as enslaved."

Accept answers that(a) California free state; Texas slave state; Oregon Territory free territory; New Mexico Territory open to slavery. (b) The South and Southeast, from Delaware and Maryland down to Florida and west to Texas, plus Missouri. (c) The census of 1850 still counted 236 people as enslaved there, bound to their owners as "apprentices", so a free state was not free for everyone.

NotesThe layer has 16 free states and 15 slave states, plus the District of Columbia. The counts are hard to make at the national view because the small eastern states are tiny and mostly unlabeled, so the question asks for groups and examples instead.

2. A line drawn in 1820

Students read the dashed line's pop-up, then find one place that breaks its rule on each side of the year 1850: Missouri, and Utah Territory.

Where to find it on the mapMissouri Compromise line pop-up: "Enacted 1820"; 36°30′ north was the northern limit of slavery in the Louisiana Territory, except Missouri, admitted as a slave state, with Maine admitted as a free state. Missouri pop-up: admitted under the Missouri Compromise of 1820, "although almost all of it lies north of the compromise line". Unorganized territory: "Closed to slavery by the Missouri Compromise of 1820, because it lies north of the compromise line." Utah Territory: "Organized by the Compromise of 1850, which left slavery for the settlers to decide."

Accept answers that(a) Slavery was not allowed north of 36°30′ in the Louisiana Territory, except in Missouri; Maine came in as a free state to keep the balance. (b) Almost all of Missouri is north of the line, but it is a slave state. (c) Unorganized territory: the Missouri Compromise of 1820 closed it to slavery. Utah Territory: the Compromise of 1850 left slavery for its settlers to decide. Strong answers notice that the dashed line stops at the edge of New Mexico Territory and is not drawn across the land organized in 1850.

NotesThe law of 1820 applied to the land of the Louisiana Purchase. Almost all of Utah and New Mexico Territories came from land Mexico gave up in 1848; eastern New Mexico had also been claimed by Texas until 1850, and Utah's pop-up notes a small area on its eastern edge that was not part of that land. Instead of extending the line of 1820, Congress wrote a different rule for the two new territories. Students don't need this to answer from the map; it explains why the dashed line stops at the edge of New Mexico Territory.

3. Before the routes appear

Before any route layer is on, students write down where they think enslaved people were being sold from and to inside the United States, and why.

Accept answers thatAny direction with a reason, for example toward newer states where land was being cleared for cotton, or toward ports. The idea is tested in question 4, so it is not marked right or wrong here.

4. Sold south

Students turn on the slave trade routes, read the direction and account for the land and sea routes, and compare what they see with what they wrote in question 3.

Where to find it on the mapRoutes of the slave trade within the United States layer and pop-ups. Overland routes: direction "South and west"; "from the Upper South, such as Virginia and Maryland, to the cotton and sugar country of the Deep South". Sea routes: "South and west, by sea"; "along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from ports in the Upper South toward New Orleans". On the map many land and sea lines meet at New Orleans, in Louisiana.

Accept answers that(a) South and west. (b) From Virginia and Maryland (the Upper South) to the cotton and sugar country of the Deep South. (c) New Orleans, in Louisiana (accept Louisiana, or the mouth of the Mississippi River). (d) Any honest comparison with the earlier idea.

NotesThe lines have no arrowheads, so the pop-up is the evidence for direction. Almost all of these routes lie inside the slave states or off their coasts. One follows the Ohio River, the border between slave states and free states; the map draws it a little north of the river, so it appears to cross the southern edge of Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. Federal law allowed this trade between the slave states in 1850. The Compromise of 1850 restricted it in one place: from January 1, 1851, nobody could bring enslaved people into Washington, D.C., to sell them.

5. Two ships

Students turn on the two ship routes and compare where each voyage ended and what happened to the people on board.

Where to find it on the mapShips La Amistad (1839) and Creole (1841) layer and pop-ups. La Amistad, 1839: from Cuba north to Long Island, New York; Africans who had been enslaved illegally took over the ship; in 1841 the Supreme Court ruled that they were free. Creole, 1841: enslaved people being shipped from Virginia to New Orleans took over the ship and sailed it to Nassau, in the British Bahamas, where most of them were freed.

Accept answers that(a) It started off Cuba and reached Long Island, New York. (b) It was going from Virginia to New Orleans; the people on board took it to Nassau, in the Bahamas. (c) The Supreme Court ruled in 1841 that the Africans from La Amistad were free; most of the people on the Creole were freed in the British Bahamas.

NotesThe Creole was sailing one of the sea routes students saw in question 4. Britain had ended slavery in its colonies in the 1830s, which is why reaching Nassau mattered.

6. Routes of escape

Students swap the trade routes for the Underground Railroad layers, follow the routes north, find the cities in Canada and measure how far beyond the Ohio River one route runs.

Where to find it on the mapUnderground Railroad approximate routes and Underground Railroad cities layers. The green lines run north and northeast from the slave states to the Great Lakes, New England and Canada, the opposite of the trade routes. Cities in Canada: Chatham and Toronto (ON) and Montreal (QC). Measure, Ripley to Chatham: about 265 miles in a straight line (accept 240 to 290). The green lines reach Montreal and the Detroit River and cross Lake Erie; they stop short of the Chatham and Toronto dots.

Accept answers that(a) North, the opposite way. (b) Chatham, Toronto and Montreal. (c) About 265 miles. (d) People kept going hundreds of miles past the free states to Canada, which suggests they were not safe from capture in a free state.

NotesThe reason is not on the map. The Constitution and a law of 1793 already let slaveholders reclaim people who had escaped to free states. The Fugitive Slave Act of September 1850, part of the Compromise of 1850, made that much easier to enforce: federal commissioners heard the claims, the person claimed could not testify, citizens could be ordered to help, and anyone who helped a person escape could be fined and jailed. Ohio has more named cities on these routes than any other state (14 of the 69).

7. What this map leaves out

Students read what the Underground Railroad pop-up says about its own routes and consider what a map drawn from an atlas of 1920 can and can't show.

Where to find it on the mapUnderground Railroad approximate routes pop-up: "An approximate route that people escaping slavery followed north. The Underground Railroad was secret, so no exact routes were recorded." The trade route pop-ups add: "The line is approximate, from a 1920 atlas map."

Accept answers that(a) The Underground Railroad was secret, so nobody recorded exact routes. (b) For example their names, how many people there were, what happened to them, or what the journey was like. (c) For example narratives written by people who escaped, letters, newspapers, ship or sale records, or census counts.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least three layers and two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised for them. Accept answers that describe the division on the map (free states in the North and California, free territories in the North and Northwest, slave states in the South, and Utah, New Mexico and Indian Territory open to slavery, with the line of 1820 and the exceptions of Missouri and Utah Territory) and say what it meant for enslaved people: being sold south and west along the trade routes, and escaping north, in many cases as far as Canada. Strong answers use New Jersey or the distance to Canada to show that free did not mean safe.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the four groups and the line of 1820, an exception (Missouri, Utah Territory or New Jersey's 236 people), the direction of the trade routes toward New Orleans, and the escape routes north to Canada (Chatham, Toronto and Montreal are marked), with the measured distance.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

By 1850 slavery split the country into two parts. On the map the free states are in the North and the slave states are in the South, and a dashed line from 1820 was supposed to keep slavery out of the land north of it. It did not settle things, because Missouri is a slave state north of the line, and Utah Territory was left for its settlers to decide. For enslaved people the split meant being moved against their will. The black routes go south and west, from Virginia and Maryland to the cotton and sugar country, and many of them meet at New Orleans. The green routes go the other way, north to Canada, where the map marks Chatham, Toronto and Montreal. Chatham is about 265 miles past the Ohio River, so crossing into a free state was not enough to be safe. Even New Jersey, a free state, still counted 236 people as enslaved.

Standards

C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
