settings.markdown:
Lessons › Civil War Battlefields

Answer notes: Civil War Battlefields

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 65 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5 to 7 and the big question
  • TopicThe Civil War (also fits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.4

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

By 1863 the United States had split in two. Where was the Civil War fought, and why there?

1. Two blues, two oranges

With only the states layer on, students read the legend, sort the states into its four groups and use pop-ups to find when the first and last states seceded.

Where to find it on the mapThe states in the Civil War, 1863 layer, legend and pop-ups. Union free state: 19. Union slave state (border state): 5 (Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, Missouri, West Virginia). Seceded before Fort Sumter: 7 (Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas). Seceded after Fort Sumter: 4 (Arkansas, North Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia). South Carolina's pop-up: December 20, 1860. Tennessee's: June 8, 1861.

Accept answers that(a) 19, 5, 7 and 4. (b) Blue is the Union; orange is the Confederacy. (c) December 20, 1860 and June 8, 1861.

NotesSouth Carolina was the first to secede and Tennessee the last; students can confirm that by clicking the other orange states. The small northeastern states are easier to count after zooming in.

2. Before the dots

Students predict where most battles were fought and write the prediction down before the battlefield layer goes on.

Accept answers thatAny prediction with a reason drawn from the map, for example along the line between blue and orange because that is where the two sides met. Question 3 tests it; it is not marked right or wrong here.

3. Turn on the battlefields

Students turn on the battlefield layer, test their prediction, and use pop-ups to find the few battlefields in Union free states.

Where to find it on the mapCivil War battlefields layer over the states layer, and battlefield pop-ups. Most dots are on orange states, and Virginia has far more than any other state. Pennsylvania's large battlefield: Gettysburg, in PA, about 73,600 acres. The dark blue (Union free) states have very few: two in Pennsylvania (Gettysburg and Hanover), two in Ohio, one in Indiana, four in Kansas and two in Minnesota.

Accept answers that(a) Orange, the states that seceded; Virginia. (b) Gettysburg, about 73,600 acres. (c) Few.

NotesCounted from the layer's state codes, not on the map: of 378 areas, 288 are in the eleven states that seceded (Virginia 121, Tennessee 38, Georgia 26; Louisiana's 23 include Yellow Bayou, whose code is mistyped L0), 62 are in the border states (Missouri 29, West Virginia 15, Kentucky 11, Maryland 7, Delaware none), 11 are in Union free states and 17 are outside the shaded states (15 named battlefields and the two unnamed areas).

4. A hundred miles apart

Students measure the distance between the two capitals, Washington, D.C. and Richmond, and use it to explain the crowd of battlefields in northern Virginia.

Where to find it on the mapMeasure, from Washington to Richmond: about 95 to 100 miles in a straight line. Battlefields layer: a dense cluster between and around the two cities, including First Manassas and Second Manassas near Washington and several around Richmond and Petersburg. Maryland's pop-up: Union slave state (border state). Virginia's: Seceded after Fort Sumter (April 1861).

Accept answers that(a) About 100 miles. (b) They are crowded together between and around the two capitals. (c) Maryland stayed in the Union and Virginia seceded; if Maryland had also seceded, Washington would have been surrounded by Confederate states.

NotesNot on the map: Washington was the United States capital and Richmond was the Confederate capital from May 1861. Each army tried to threaten the other side's capital and protect its own, which is one reason so much fighting happened in the ground between them.

5. Follow the rails

Students turn on the railroads at the same bookmark, compare the networks north and south, and check whether battlefields sit on rail lines.

Where to find it on the mapRailroads in operation by 1863 layer with the battlefields on. Pennsylvania and Ohio are covered by a dense web of lines; Virginia and North Carolina have fewer, longer lines with wide gaps. The battlefields at Manassas and Petersburg both sit where railroad lines meet.

Accept answers that(a) The blue, Union side. (b) Both are at places where railroads cross or join. (c) Railroads carried soldiers, food and ammunition, so holding a junction helped one army and cut off the other.

NotesSummed from the layer, not on the map: about 23,000 miles of track in the Union states and about 9,000 miles in the states that seceded. The railroads only draw once the map is zoomed in to a region.

6. Down the Mississippi

Students move to the Mississippi Valley, find the string of battlefields along the river and work out what control of the river would do to the Confederacy.

Where to find it on the mapBattlefields layer and pop-ups at The Mississippi Valley bookmark. On or beside the river, north to south: New Madrid Island No 10 (MO), Fort Pillow and Memphis (TN), Helena (AR), Vicksburg and Grand Gulf (MS), Port Hudson, Baton Rouge and New Orleans (LA). States layer: Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas are west of the river (part of Louisiana is east of it). Other areas on the river are also correct, for example Belmont (MO), Milliken's Bend, Goodrich's Landing, Donaldsonville and Forts Jackson & St. Phillip (LA). Memphis appears as Memphis I and Memphis II.

Accept answers that(a) Any three battlefields on the river, such as those named. (b) Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas. (c) They would be cut off from the rest of the Confederacy, and the Union could move troops and supplies along the river.

NotesVicksburg's pop-up gives about 38,600 acres. The Battle of Vicksburg lesson picks up from here.

7. What the dots leave out

Students find battlefields outside the shaded states and decide what the layer can and cannot tell them.

Where to find it on the mapBattlefields layer at the national view: dots in today's North Dakota, Oklahoma, New Mexico, Colorado and Idaho, none of them on a shaded state. Almost every battlefield pop-up gives the name, the state and the acres (two unnamed areas in Oklahoma do not), and each ends: "This layer does not say who won."

Accept answers that(a) Any of those places, for example North Dakota or New Mexico. (b) It gives the name, the state and the size of the area; it leaves out the date, who fought, who won and how many people were killed or wounded. (c) A National Park Service battle summary, a textbook, letters or newspapers from the time.

NotesTeacher notes say more about the western sites, which include fights between United States troops and Native nations and two massacres of Native people, at Bear River and Sand Creek.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from all three layers and at least one measurement or pop-up, then write one "why" question the map raised. Accept answers that say most battles were fought in the states that seceded and the border states, above all Virginia; that the ground between Washington and Richmond, railroad junctions and the Mississippi River drew the armies; and that few battles reached the Union free states.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the states layer (the four groups and which states border Washington), the battlefields layer (most dots on orange states, Virginia the most, Gettysburg as a rare battle in a free state), the Washington to Richmond measurement, the railroads (denser in the Union, junctions at Manassas and Petersburg) and the river battlefields.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

Most of the Civil War was fought in the South, and a lot of it in Virginia. When I turned on the battlefields, almost all the dots were on the orange states, and Virginia had the most by far. The dark blue states had only a few, like Gettysburg in Pennsylvania, which the pop-up says is about 73,600 acres. I think Virginia had so many because of the capitals. I measured from Washington to Richmond and it was only about 100 miles, and the battlefields are packed in between. The railroads matter too. The Union states have way more purple lines, and Manassas and Petersburg are both where rail lines meet, so armies fought over them. In the Mississippi Valley the battlefields follow the river, like Vicksburg and Port Hudson. If the Union held the river, Texas, Arkansas and Louisiana were cut off. So the war was fought where the capitals, railroads and rivers were.

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.10(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
FL SS.8.A.5.4Framework: FloridaStandard: Identify the division (Confederate and Union States, Border states, western territories) of the United States at the outbreak of the Civil War

Answer notes: The Battle of Vicksburg

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicThe Civil War
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • FL SS.8.A.5.1

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Why did the Union need Vicksburg, and how did Grant take it?

1. Why Vicksburg?

Open The Battle of Vicksburg bookmark. Vicksburg is the yellow pin. Look at where it sits on the Mississippi River. Find the railroad line and follow it east from Vicksburg to Jackson, Mississippi, the state capital, which is a basemap label (not a pin) just past the bookmark's east edge. Why would both sides want the city?

Where to find it on the mapThe Battle of Vicksburg bookmark; yellow pin at Vicksburg on a bend of the Mississippi; Railroads 1826 to 1911 layer, which already draws at the bookmark and disappears when zoomed out past about 1:1,500,000; Jackson is a label on the Modern Antique basemap about 40 miles east, just beyond the bookmark's east edge, so students drag the map to reach it.

Accept answers thatSays Vicksburg sits on the river, so whoever held it controlled traffic on the Mississippi, and that its railroad linked the river to Jackson and the rest of the Confederacy, so it was both a river stronghold and a rail junction. Mentioning the bluffs or guns is extra, not on the map.

2. Grant's route

Find the dark pins and put them in order along Grant's route: Milliken's Bend (spelled Miliken's Bend on the map, at the top edge of the bookmark's view), New Carthage, Hard Times, Bruinsburg Bend, then Edwards. Which side of the river is each on? Measure the straight-line distance from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend.

Where to find it on the mapKey Places in the Union March to Vicksburg pins, read against the river and the basemap state labels: Milliken's Bend, New Carthage and Hard Times are on the west (Louisiana) bank; Bruinsburg Bend and Edwards are on the east (Mississippi) side. Measure tool, Milliken's Bend pin to Bruinsburg Bend pin: about 33 miles in a straight line (accept 31 to 36).

Accept answers thatNotices that Vicksburg's pin sits on the river between Milliken's Bend (north) and Bruinsburg Bend (south), so Grant could not cross right at the city; he marched down the far bank, out of reach of the city, crossed well to the south, then turned back toward Vicksburg from the east (Edwards).

3. The battles of May 1863

Turn on Civil War Battlefields in Map layers and click the diamonds between Bruinsburg Bend and Vicksburg, and east toward Jackson. Put the battles in order by date from the pop-ups.

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefields pop-ups: the name is in bold and the dates below it. Grand Gulf (April 29, 1863), on the river just north of Bruinsburg, is the Union navy's failed attack before the crossing; accept it if students include it.

Accept answers thatThe battles in date order (see the table). No: after Port Gibson the dates lead east to Raymond and Jackson (May 12 and 14), then back west through Champion Hill and Big Black River Bridge (May 16 and 17) to Vicksburg (May 18), so Grant reached Vicksburg from the east.

Answer key
BattleDates
Port GibsonDates: May 1, 1863
RaymondDates: May 12, 1863
Jackson, MississippiDates: May 14, 1863
Champion HillDates: May 16, 1863
Big Black River BridgeDates: May 17, 1863
VicksburgDates: May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863

4. Splitting the Confederacy

Zoom out to see the whole Mississippi River from Memphis to the Gulf. With Civil War Battlefields on, click the diamond at Port Hudson, Louisiana, south of Vicksburg, for its dates. Using the state names on the basemap, which states lie west of the river, and what did the Union control once both Vicksburg and Port Hudson had surrendered?

Where to find it on the mapCivil War Battlefields pop-up for Port Hudson: May 21, 1863 – July 9, 1863. Vicksburg pop-up: May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863. Basemap state labels west of the river: Louisiana (most of it), Arkansas, Texas (and Missouri further north, Union side).

Accept answers thatPort Hudson surrendered on July 9, 1863, five days after Vicksburg. Names Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas west of the river and says the Union then controlled the whole Mississippi, so those Confederate states were cut off from the rest of the Confederacy and the river was open to Union ships and closed to Confederate supplies.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two places on the map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, Grant's route sketched on the map (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the yellow Vicksburg pin on the Mississippi and the railroad east to the Jackson basemap label, the dark Key Places pins in order (Milliken's Bend to Edwards) with Measure from Milliken's Bend to Bruinsburg Bend (about 33 miles), and dates from the Civil War Battlefields pop-ups (Port Gibson, May 1, 1863; Vicksburg, May 18, 1863 – July 4, 1863; Port Hudson, to July 9, 1863).

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The Union needed Vicksburg because it controlled the Mississippi River, and Grant took it by going around it. Vicksburg sits on a bend of the river, and a railroad runs east from it to Jackson, so it linked the river to the rest of the Confederacy. Grant did not cross at the city. He marched down the Louisiana side from Milliken's Bend to New Carthage and Hard Times, and crossed at Bruinsburg Bend, about 33 miles south in a straight line. Then he went east, not straight to Vicksburg. The battles were Port Gibson on May 1, Raymond on May 12, Jackson on May 14, Champion Hill on May 16 and Big Black River Bridge on May 17, 1863. The siege of Vicksburg lasted from May 18 to July 4. Port Hudson fell on July 9, so the Union held the whole river, and Louisiana, Arkansas and Texas were cut off.

C3 D2.His.14.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
TX 8.10(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
FL SS.8.A.5.1Framework: FloridaStandard: Explain the causes, course, and consequence of the Civil War (sectionalism, slavery, states' rights, balance of power in the Senate)

Answer notes: We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicConfederation and the Constitution (also fits: The early republic)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Civ.5.6-8

    • TX 8.4(D)

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Who was counted in the new Constitution, and how close did it come to being rejected?

1. Who lived where in 1790?

Open The states in 1790 bookmark. Students compare the pie sizes to find the most populous state, then click the pies and read the 1790 census line of each pop-up to find the states where more than a quarter of the people were enslaved.

Where to find it on the mapThe states in 1790 bookmark; Population in 1790 layer. Biggest pie and pop-up first line: Virginia, 747,610 people (Kentucky is counted separately; Massachusetts, which then included Maine, is next with 475,327). The percentage in the first line of each pop-up ("1790 census: … people, … of them enslaved (…%)") is above 25 in five states, listed below. Legend: blue = free people, orange-red = enslaved people.

Answer key
StatePeopleEnslavedShare enslaved
South CarolinaPeople: 249,073Enslaved: 107,094Share enslaved: 43.0%
VirginiaPeople: 747,610Enslaved: 292,627Share enslaved: 39.1%
GeorgiaPeople: 82,548Enslaved: 29,264Share enslaved: 35.5%
MarylandPeople: 319,728Enslaved: 103,036Share enslaved: 32.2%

NotesThe pop-up shows some percentages with many decimal places (Virginia reads 39.099998474121094%, Maryland 32.20000076293945%); accept the rounded figure.

2. Seats in Congress

Turn on House seats in 1793. Students use the labels (abbreviation and seats) and the legend to find the states with the most and fewest seats, then read the pop-up to compare House seats with senators.

Where to find it on the mapHouse seats in 1793 layer. Labels and legend (darkest class, 13 to 19 seats): Virginia, VA: 19, the most of the 105 seats. Palest class (1 to 2 seats): Delaware, DE: 1, the fewest; Vermont, Rhode Island, Kentucky and Georgia have 2. Pop-up, second paragraph: "plus 2 senators, like every state".

Accept answers thatNames Virginia (19) and Delaware (1), says every state had two senators, and explains the Great Compromise in its own words: House seats follow population, which suited the large states, while the equal Senate protected the small ones. The pop-up also gives the ratio, one seat for every 33,000 people counted.

3. The three-fifths clause

Students click Virginia and South Carolina and read the paragraph of each pop-up that begins "If enslaved people had been counted in full", which gives the seats each would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all, and compare them with the actual seats. Then they look for other states where the two numbers differ.

Where to find it on the mapPopulation in 1790 or House seats in 1793 pop-up, the sentence "That gave … House seats in 1793" and the third paragraph, which begins "If enslaved people had been counted in full" and goes on to the count if they had not been counted at all. A note about state outlines and a line of source links come after it. Virginia: 19, 22, 13. South Carolina: 6, 7, 4. Seven states show a higher seat count under the clause than with no count, listed below.

Accept answers thatGives Virginia 19, 22 and 13 (fill-in) and South Carolina 6, 7 and 4, names at least Virginia, North Carolina, Maryland and South Carolina as states that gained seats, and says that enslaved people were counted for seats but could not vote, so the gain went to the slaveholding states. The seven states gained 15 seats in all (105 instead of 90), Virginia alone 6.

New YorkSeats (three-fifths): 10If counted in full: 10If not counted: 9
GeorgiaSeats (three-fifths): 2If counted in full: 2If not counted: 1
KentuckySeats (three-fifths): 2If counted in full: 2If not counted: 1

4. How close was ratification?

Turn off Population in 1790 and House seats in 1793 and turn on Ratifying the Constitution. Students click the pies, read the vote line of each pop-up ("Ratified on …: … for, … against") to find the three closest votes, and open both North Carolina pies to explain why there are two.

Where to find it on the mapRatifying the Constitution layer; legend: blue = voted to ratify, orange-red = voted against. Pop-up first line: Rhode Island 34 for, 32 against (label RI 13, May 29, 1790); New York 30–27 (NY 11, July 26, 1788); Massachusetts 187–168 (MA 6, February 6, 1788). By number of votes the next closest are Virginia 89–79 (VA 10) and New Hampshire 57–47 (NH 9, the ninth state, enough to put the Constitution into effect). North Carolina: the NC (1788) pie at Hillsborough, titled "Did not ratify (first convention)", 83 for, 184 against, with a note that a second convention ratified in November 1789; the NC 12 pie at Fayetteville, 194–77, November 21, 1789.

Accept answers thatNames Rhode Island, New York and Massachusetts (accept Virginia or New Hampshire if the student counts the gap in votes rather than the share), and explains that North Carolina's first convention did not ratify and a second one did more than a year later, after Congress had proposed the Bill of Rights. Sources differ on the exact 1788 vote and date; accept the pop-up's figures.

The dates given here are the correct ones, so a date one day early read from the pop-up is not a student error. The vote counts are not affected.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers: one number about representation (House seats, senators or the three-fifths lines of a pop-up) and one ratification vote. A paragraph or a short talk using the map both work.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the House seats in 1793 labels, legend and pop-ups (Virginia VA: 19, Delaware DE: 1, and 2 senators for every state), the three-fifths lines of a pop-up (Virginia 19 seats, 22 if counted in full, 13 if not counted), and the vote line of the Ratifying the Constitution pop-ups (Rhode Island 34–32 on May 29, 1790; New York 30–27; Massachusetts 187–168).

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The Constitution counted people in two different ways, and it only just passed. Every state got two senators, but House seats followed population, so Virginia had 19 seats and Delaware had 1. Enslaved people were counted as three-fifths even though they could not vote. That gave Virginia 19 seats when it would have had 13 if enslaved people had not been counted, and South Carolina 6 where it would have had 4. So the extra seats went to slaveholding states. Ratification was close in some states. Rhode Island voted 34 to 32, New York 30 to 27 and Massachusetts 187 to 168. North Carolina's first convention did not ratify, and a second one did in November 1789. Delaware voted 30 to 0, so the fight was much harder in some states than in others.

Answer notes: Rights and Responsibilities Where We Live

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicConfederation and the Constitution (also fits: The early republic)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards

    • C3 D2.Civ.8.6-8
    • C3 D2.Geo.1.6-8
    • TX 8.19(B)
    • TX 8.19(C)
    • FL SS.8.CG.2.5

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Where in our community do people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities?

1. Who represents us?

Students zoom to their town on the Topographic basemap and click inside their congressional district to read the pop-up, which names the representative, their party and the district number. Then they zoom out to the whole state and count the blue-outlined districts.

Where to find it on the mapCongressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up: "[Representative Name] ([Party]) represents [State] Congressional District [number]". The district count is the number of blue-outlined areas in the state when zoomed out, which equals the state's House seats after the 2020 census: for example California 52, Texas 38, Florida 28; six states (Alaska, Delaware, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming) have one, shown as the whole state.

Accept answers thatAccept the name and party as the pop-up gives them for the 119th Congress (2025–2027); a seat that has changed hands since the layer was updated may differ. A vacant seat shows no name and "Vacant" as the party (Florida's 20th and Texas's 23rd when checked on November 11, 2026), and one California district showed an empty party. States with one seat show district 00; the District of Columbia and the territories show 98. In California, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee, Texas and Utah the district on the November 2026 ballot may differ from the one shown (see the map's description).

2. Rights in public places

Students zoom in on their town until the Topographic basemap labels buildings, pick four public places it shows or that they know (courthouse, city hall, library, place of worship, polling place, newspaper office), sketch a pin on each and label it with a right from the Bill of Rights that people use there. Sketches are not saved, so students finish in one session or take a screenshot.

Where to find it on the mapThe Topographic basemap labels schools, churches, courthouses, libraries and city halls in most towns at close zoom. Sketch tool: a pin and a text label at each place. There is no stored answer; the teacher checks the student's screen or screenshot.

Accept answers thatFour pins on public places (not homes), each paired with a right that fits: a newspaper office with freedom of the press, a place of worship with free exercise of religion, city hall or a public square with assembly and petition, a library with speech and the press, a courthouse with due process or a jury trial (Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Amendments). A polling place connects with voting, which later amendments protect (15th, 19th and 26th), so accept it with that note.

3. Responsibilities

Students start from the courthouse or city hall they pinned in question 2 and add pins for places where people carry out responsibilities as citizens (voting, jury service, paying taxes). Which are required by law and which are voluntary is a question for the class discussion.

Where to find it on the mapSketch pins on the student's map, usually at the courthouse (jury service), a polling place such as a school, library or church (voting), and a post office or tax office (paying taxes). There is no stored answer; check the screen or screenshot.

Accept answers thatAt least two pins with a responsibility each. For the discussion: obeying laws, paying taxes, jury service when called and, for most men aged 18 through 25, Selective Service registration are required by law; voting, staying informed, volunteering and attending community meetings are voluntary. Accept the point that voting is both a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it.

4. History where we live

Turn on National Register of Historic Places, zoom in until the diamonds appear, and click the two nearest the school. The pop-up gives each place's name and address. Look for a public building and the right or responsibility it connects with.

Where to find it on the mapNational Register of Historic Places layer, on at close zoom. Pop-up: the place's name in bold, then address, city, county, state, resource type and a National Archive Information link. Legend: diamond colors for building, structure, district, site and object. If nothing is listed nearby, zoom out to the nearest town.

Accept answers thatTwo places identified by name, with a sensible link for any public building: a courthouse with jury service and a fair trial; a post office or newspaper building with sharing news and ideas; a school or library with staying informed. Accept "neither is a public building" with a reason.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from their own map. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a screenshot of the sketched map with a short caption, or a short talk using the map. Sketches are not saved between sessions.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers name places on the student's own map: the representative, party and district number from the Congressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up; public buildings the Topographic basemap labels at close zoom (courthouse, city hall, library, polling place) with the student's Sketch pins; and a National Register of Historic Places diamond identified by its pop-up address and legend type.

Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

In my town, people use their rights and carry out their responsibilities in a few public buildings near the center. My first pin is the county courthouse. People have the right to a jury trial there, and serving on a jury when called is required by law. My second pin is the public library, where anyone can read and share ideas, so I labeled it freedom of speech and of the press. My third pin is my school, which is our polling place. Voting is a right and a responsibility, but no federal law requires it. The Congressional districts pop-up names the person who represents our district in the House of Representatives. One of the historic places near my school is the old courthouse, so people have used their rights in the same place for a long time.

C3 D2.Geo.1.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Construct maps to represent and explain the spatial patterns of cultural and environmental characteristics.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › The First Political Parties, 1796–1800

Answer notes: The First Political Parties, 1796–1800

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 57 minutes: 47 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicThe early republic
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • TX 8.5(D)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.13
    • FL SS.8.A.3.14

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the first political parties divide the country?

1. The election of 1796

Open The sixteen states bookmark and turn off Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819, whose squares cover Maryland's pie. Use the pies and the legend to find which regions mostly voted for Adams and which for Jefferson, and click the two-color pies for the split states' numbers.

Where to find it on the mapThe sixteen states bookmark; Election of 1796: electors' votes layer. With Landmark Supreme Court cases, 1803 and 1819 left on, a click on Maryland's pie opens a court case first. Legend: orange = John Adams, blue = Thomas Jefferson; the pop-up names the state. All-orange pies: Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont. All-blue: Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina, Tennessee. Two-color pies, from the pop-up's 1796 votes line: Maryland (Adams 7, Jefferson 4), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14, Adams 1), Virginia (Jefferson 20, Adams 1), North Carolina (Jefferson 11, Adams 1).

Accept answers thatAdams: New England and the states around New York (New York, New Jersey, Delaware). Jefferson: the South and the West, plus most of Pennsylvania. The four split states named, with Maryland the only split state Adams won.

NotesThe totals are not on the map: Adams 71, Jefferson 68, so Jefferson, the runner-up, became vice president.

2. The election of 1800

Turn off Election of 1796 and turn on Election of 1800. Find the two-color pies and click each for the numbers; identify the closest state.

Where to find it on the mapElection of 1800: electors' votes layer; two-color pies, pop-up 1800 votes line: Maryland (Jefferson 5, Adams 5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 8, Adams 7), North Carolina (Jefferson 8, Adams 4). Closest: Maryland, an even split.

NotesEvery 1800 pop-up says that Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied with 73 votes each; Adams's total, 65, is not on the map. Each elector cast two votes, so the pop-ups also list Burr and Charles C. Pinckney.

3. Which states switched?

Compare the two elections by switching between Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 in Map layers. Find the state whose whole pie changed color, the states whose shares changed, and describe where each party was strong.

Where to find it on the mapElection of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers, pop-up title (state and number of electors) and votes lines. New York, 12 electors: all Adams in 1796, all Jefferson in 1800. Shares changed: Maryland (Adams 7–4 to 5–5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 14–1 to 8–7), North Carolina (Jefferson 11–1 to 8–4), Virginia (Jefferson 20–1 to 21–0). No New England state changed: Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont stayed all orange.

Accept answers thatNames New York as the only state that switched entirely; notes that the middle states (Maryland, Pennsylvania, North Carolina) were split in both elections; says the Federalists were strong in New England and the Democratic-Republicans in the South and West, with the middle states (and New York) deciding the result.

NotesNew York's 12 votes were more than the margin: without that switch Adams would have had 77 votes to Jefferson's 61 in 1800, instead of 65 to 73.

4. Did one state decide the election?

With Election of 1800 on, students click New York and the split states, read the electors' votes, and work out what the result would have been if New York had voted as it did in 1796.

Where to find it on the mapElection of 1800: electors' votes layer. New York pop-up title: 12 electors, all for Jefferson in 1800 (all for Adams in 1796). Moving those 12 gives Adams 65 + 12 = 77 and Jefferson 73 − 12 = 61. Split states, from the 1800 votes line: Maryland (Jefferson 5, Adams 5), Pennsylvania (Jefferson 8, Adams 7), North Carolina (Jefferson 8, Adams 4).

Accept answers thatAdams 77, Jefferson 61: New York's switch was enough to decide the election. Maryland (5 to 5) and Pennsylvania (8 to 7) were the closest states. A swing of five electors anywhere would also have reversed the result (65 + 5 = 70 against 73 − 5 = 68), so accept either state with that reasoning.

NotesJefferson's 73 is in every 1800 pop-up (the tie with Burr), but Adams's 65 is not on the map, so the question gives both totals. Each elector cast two votes, which is why Jefferson and Burr tied at 73; the pop-ups explain it.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from both election layers. Accept answers that name a region for each party and use the split states or New York's switch as evidence. A paragraph, or a sketch that marks each party's region (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), both work.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the pies and legend of the Election of 1796 and Election of 1800 layers (orange for Adams, blue for Jefferson) with numbers from the pop-ups, such as New York's 12 electors switching from all Adams to all Jefferson, Maryland 7–4 then 5–5 and Pennsylvania 14–1 then 8–7.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The first parties split the country by region. In 1796 every New England state voted for Adams, the Federalist. Georgia, Kentucky, South Carolina and Tennessee all voted for Jefferson. The states in the middle were divided. Maryland gave Adams 7 votes and Jefferson 4, and four years later it split 5 to 5. Pennsylvania went from 14 to 1 for Jefferson to 8 to 7. The biggest change was New York. All 12 of its electors voted for Adams in 1796 and all 12 voted for Jefferson in 1800. No New England state changed at all. So each party had a region it could count on, and the election was decided in a few states between them.

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
TX 8.5(D)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Explain the origin and development of American political parties
FL SS.8.A.3.13Framework: FloridaStandard: Explain major domestic and international economic, military, political, and socio-cultural events of John Adams's presidency.
FL SS.8.A.3.14Framework: FloridaStandard: Explain major domestic and international economic, military, political, and socio-cultural events of Thomas Jefferson's presidency.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

Answer notes: The Louisiana Purchase and the Corps of Discovery, 1803–1806

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicThe early republic (also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.10(C)
    • TX 8.6(B)
    • FL SS.8.A.3.14
    • FL SS.8.G.1.2

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

What did the Louisiana Purchase add to the United States, and why did the Mississippi River matter so much?

1. A bigger country

Open The Louisiana Purchase bookmark. Use the legend to compare the yellow Louisiana Purchase with the green land of 1783, and click the purchase for its size and price.

Where to find it on the mapThe Louisiana Purchase bookmark; Territorial acquisitions to 1803 layer. Legend: green = Territory of the Original Thirteen States (Ceded by Great Britain) 1783, yellow = Louisiana Purchase 1803. Louisiana Purchase 1803 pop-up, Notes: 530,000,000 acres, bought from France in 1803 for $15 million. Fill-in: 530 million acres, $15 million.

Accept answers thatAbout double, or roughly the same size as the country before it. The layer's data agrees (about 2.1 million km² for the purchase and 2.3 million km² for the 1783 land), but the pop-up does not show the area, so students judge it by eye.

NotesSome edges were settled later and have their own legend entries and pop-ups: the strip ceded to Great Britain in 1818 (striped), and the parts that came with Texas in 1845 and the Mexican Cession in 1848.

2. Why New Orleans?

Turn on United States Watersheds. Click inside the two large brown outlines along the Ohio and the Missouri to name the regions, then follow the rivers on the basemap to find where their water reaches the sea, and explain why New Orleans mattered to western farmers.

Where to find it on the mapUnited States Watersheds layer, at the bookmark's scale (zoomed out, the brown outlines are the largest regions; if the pop-up says 1 of 2, the region is the entry whose HUC ID has two digits). Pop-up, first line: Ohio Region (Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana and nearby states) and Missouri Region (the Great Plains). On the basemap both rivers join the Mississippi, which reaches the Gulf of Mexico at New Orleans; the city is not labeled, so students find the river mouth. Also accept Upper Mississippi Region or Arkansas-White-Red Region if clicked.

Accept answers thatNames both regions; says their rivers flow into the Mississippi and so past New Orleans to the sea; explains that whoever held New Orleans could stop or tax western farmers' crops on the way to market, so the United States needed the port.

NotesZoomed in, the layer shows smaller watersheds with their own names; ask students to zoom out until the outlines are the large regions. In 1802 Spanish officials at New Orleans stopped Americans storing goods in the port, and Jefferson tried to buy New Orleans before France offered all of Louisiana.

3. Up the Missouri

Open the Up the Missouri bookmark, follow the trail line and campsites upriver, turn off Watersheds and turn on Biomes, and click along the route for the biome's name.

Where to find it on the mapUp the Missouri bookmark; Biomes layer, pop-up first line (also in the legend): Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands along the Missouri across the Great Plains. The biome stays grassland along the Missouri all the way through Montana; Temperate Conifer Forests begins only where the trail climbs into the Rockies, west of this bookmark's view. The campsite symbols sit on the riverbanks.

Accept answers thatNames the grassland biome; gives a reason for following rivers, such as travel by boat, drinking water, food, or a route through open country without roads or maps.

4. Across the Rockies

Turn off Biomes, which hides the yellow purchase, and open the Across the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark. Note where the trail leaves the yellow purchase, then measure the straight-line distance from the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh to its western end on the Pacific coast.

Where to find it on the mapAcross the Rockies to the Pacific bookmark, with Biomes turned off (it draws over the purchase and hides the yellow); Territorial acquisitions to 1803 layer with the legend: the trail crosses out of the yellow purchase in the Rocky Mountains (the Continental Divide, on the Montana–Idaho border) and the Pacific Northwest is unshaded, so it was not part of the purchase. Measure tool, Pittsburgh to the trail's end at the mouth of the Columbia River: about 2,200 miles (accept 2,100 to 2,300).

Accept answers thatSays the trail leaves the purchase at the Rockies and the Pacific coast was outside it; a measured distance in the accepted range; may note that the straight line is less than half the trail's 4,900 miles because the Corps followed winding rivers and mountain passes.

NotesThe basemap has no place names: Pittsburgh is where the trail line starts, at the fork where the Ohio River begins; the western end is where the line reaches the ocean.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Accept answers that give the purchase's size and price from the pop-up and use the watersheds, rivers or trail as evidence of what the land offered (rivers to the Gulf, plains, a route west) and why New Orleans and the Mississippi mattered to western farmers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; sketch pins for New Orleans and for two places on the trail, with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. The question of whose land this was is in Looking back: the map has no Native nations layer, so it is answered from Before you start (the Corps met more than 50 Tribal Nations) and reasoning, not from the map.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the Louisiana Purchase 1803 pop-up Notes (530,000,000 acres, $15 million) against the legend's green land of 1783, the United States Watersheds pop-ups (Ohio Region, Missouri Region) traced on the basemap to the Mississippi and New Orleans, the Biomes pop-up (Temperate Grasslands, Savannas & Shrublands) and a Measure distance from Pittsburgh to the Pacific of about 2,200 miles.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The Louisiana Purchase about doubled the United States, and the Mississippi mattered because it was the way to market for farmers in the West. On the map the yellow purchase is about the same size as the green land the country had in 1783. Its pop-up says it was 530,000,000 acres, bought from France in 1803 for $15 million. The watershed layer shows why the river mattered. The Ohio Region and the Missouri Region both drain into the Mississippi, which reaches the Gulf of Mexico at New Orleans. Whoever held New Orleans could stop or tax crops on their way to the sea. Lewis and Clark followed the Missouri across grasslands, and their trail leaves the purchase at the Rocky Mountains, so the Pacific coast was not part of it. The map has no layer for the Native nations who lived on this land.

Standards

CodeFrameworkStandard
C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.
TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.10(C)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
TX 8.6(B)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the westward growth of the nation, including the Louisiana Purchase and Manifest Destiny
FL SS.8.A.3.14Framework: FloridaStandard: Explain major domestic and international economic, military, political, and socio-cultural events of Thomas Jefferson's presidency.
FL SS.8.G.1.2Framework: FloridaStandard: Use appropriate geographic tools and terms to identify and describe significant places and regions in American history.

pages.title: Answer notes: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823
pages.summary: Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept, for the MapMaker lesson The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823. For teachers.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

Answer notes: The War of 1812 and the Monroe Doctrine, 1807–1823

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 59 minutes: 49 for the questions and 10 to write the answer. One question on its own takes 10–15
  • TopicThe early republic (also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.1.6-8
    • TX 8.5(E)
    • TX 8.5(F)
    • FL SS.8.A.4.1

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the War of 1812 and the years after it change the United States' place in North and South America?

1. Where was the war fought?

Open The War of 1812 bookmark and use the battle diamonds to find the three main areas of fighting.

Where to find it on the mapThe War of 1812 bookmark; Battles of the War of 1812 layer. The pop-up gives the battle's name, dates and account; it does not name the state, and the basemap has no place names. The legend gives the result by color. Students place each group from the map itself: around the Great Lakes and the border with British Canada, around Chesapeake Bay, and near the Gulf Coast and in Alabama. Some accounts mention a place, which helps.

Accept answers thatThree areas named by region, read from the shape of the coast and lakes or from places the pop-up accounts mention: the Canadian border and Great Lakes; the Chesapeake Bay area around Washington and Baltimore; the South along the Gulf Coast and in Alabama. Accept the Creek War battles in Alabama as part of the southern area.

NotesAround Chesapeake Bay the British won at Bladensburg and burned Washington, then failed to take Baltimore. The Alabama battles were the Creek War against the Red Stick Creeks. The layer also includes Tippecanoe (November 1811), fought before the war against a Native confederacy; the pop-up may say 1 of 2 because the click also lands on the Historic National Boundaries layer (its pop-up reads Year 1800). The tan battlefield land draws only when zoomed in close, so there is none at this bookmark.

2. The biggest battles

Click the largest diamonds to find the battles with the most casualties, their dates and results, and compare the date of New Orleans with the Treaty of Ghent.

Where to find it on the mapBattles of the War of 1812 layer, the three largest diamonds: in each pop-up, the dates under the title, the victor line (American Side Victory, British Side Victory or Inconclusive) and Total Casualties. The pop-up does not show the state; the places in the table are for the teacher. Legend: blue = American victory, red = British victory, gray = inconclusive. The table lists the five largest in case students pick a different third.

Accept answers thatThe three battles with the most casualties, each with its date and result from the pop-up and a place worked out from the map or the account (the Niagara River or Canadian border for Fort Erie and Lundy's Lane); New Orleans (January 8, 1815) identified as the battle fought after the Treaty of Ghent.

Answer key
BattleDatesResultCasualties
Siege of Fort Erie (Ontario)Dates: August 4 – September 21, 1814Result: American victoryCasualties: 2,628
New Orleans (Louisiana)Dates: January 8, 1815Result: American victoryCasualties: 2,096
Lundy's Lane (Ontario)Dates: July 25, 1814Result: InconclusiveCasualties: 1,731
Horseshoe Bend (Alabama)Dates: March 27, 1814Result: American victory over the Red Stick CreeksCasualties: 1,339
Queenston Heights (Ontario)Dates: October 13, 1812Result: British victoryCasualties: 1,233

NotesFort Erie, New Orleans and Lundy's Lane are the three largest; news of the peace hadn't crossed the Atlantic before New Orleans. Horseshoe Bend (fourth largest) was fought against the Red Stick Creeks, not the British: the legend's British label is the layer's simplification, and the pop-up's account names Menawa and the Red Sticks.

3. Florida and a new border

Open The 1819 boundary bookmark, turn on Land Spain gave up in 1819 and the Adams–Onís Treaty line, and read their pop-ups to describe what the treaty settled.

Where to find it on the mapThe 1819 boundary bookmark. Land Spain gave up in 1819 layer: green areas East Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819, West Florida (Spanish Cession) 1819 and Spanish Cession 1819; the Notes in each pop-up say the land came through the Adams-Onís Treaty and instead of paying Spain, the United States took on $5 million, which the pop-up describes as damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain; the treaty's own terms are claims by American citizens against Spain. Adams–Onís Treaty line, 1819 layer, pop-ups part 1 to part 7: the Sabine River north to 32° N; north to the Red River; the Red River west to 100° W; north along 100° W to the Arkansas River; the Arkansas upstream to its source; north to 42° N; west along 42° N to the Pacific.

Accept answers thatFlorida (East and West) gained from Spain, with the $5 million if read. Rivers: the Sabine, the Red and the Arkansas. Straight lines: north to the Red River, 100° W, north to 42° N, and 42° N to the Pacific. For why, accept any reasoned answer, for example that a river is a landmark both sides can find, and where no river ran the right way the treaty used lines of latitude and longitude.

NotesThe United States already held much of West Florida. The treaty was signed in 1819 and ratified in 1821. The line is drawn from the treaty's description and is approximate, as each pop-up's note says.

4. New nations and the Monroe Doctrine

Open Latin America in 1825, turn on the independence layer, and compare the dates of independence and US recognition with President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823.

Where to find it on the mapLatin America in 1825 bookmark; Latin American independence and US recognition layer (legend: blue circle = recognized by the United States by 1824, orange diamond = recognized later). Six blue circles; the pop-up's US recognition line gives the date. Before December 2, 1823: Republic of Colombia (June 19, 1822), Mexico (December 12, 1822), Buenos Ayres (January 27, 1823) and Chile (January 27, 1823). Brazil (May 26, 1824) and the Federation of Central America (August 4, 1824) are blue but were recognized after the message.

Accept answers thatThe four nations recognized before the message, read from the pop-up dates (not all six blue circles); a reason for the warning that uses the map, such as new independent nations across the Americas that European powers might try to take back, or the United States wanting to be the main power in the region.

Answer key
NationIndependenceRecognized by the United States
Republic of ColombiaIndependence: 1819Recognized by the United States: June 19, 1822
MexicoIndependence: 1821Recognized by the United States: December 12, 1822
Buenos Ayres (Argentina)Independence: 1816Recognized by the United States: January 27, 1823
ChileIndependence: 1818Recognized by the United States: January 27, 1823
BrazilIndependence: 1822Recognized by the United States: May 26, 1824
Federation of Central AmericaIndependence: 1821Recognized by the United States: August 4, 1824

NotesThe pop-up shows each recognition date as a date and time in the computer's time zone, so in the United States it reads the evening before (Mexico shows 12/11/1822, not December 12). The dates given here are the correct ones, and which nations fall before December 2, 1823 does not change. Monroe warned European powers not to set up new colonies in the Americas or interfere with the newly independent nations, and said the United States would stay out of Europe's wars. Haiti, independent since 1804, was not recognized until 1862 (orange diamond).

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph; a sketch of the three war fronts and of the 1819 border and the area the Monroe Doctrine covered (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them); or a short talk using the map. Accept answers that use the battles to show the war ended without gains, the 1819 layers to show the United States growing and fixing its border with Spain, and the independence layer to show the new nations the Monroe Doctrine spoke for.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the Battles of the War of 1812 pop-ups (the victor line and Total Casualties: Fort Erie 2,628; New Orleans, January 8, 1815, after the Treaty of Ghent of December 24, 1814), the Land Spain gave up in 1819 and Adams–Onís Treaty line pop-ups (East and West Florida; Sabine River, 100° W, 42° N) and the Latin American independence pop-ups (Mexico recognized December 12, 1822).

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The war itself changed little, but in the years after it the United States grew and began to speak for the Americas. The battles were in three areas: along the Great Lakes and the Canadian border, around Chesapeake Bay, and in the South near the Gulf Coast. One of the biggest battles, New Orleans, was fought on January 8, 1815, after the peace treaty was signed on December 24, 1814. In 1819 Spain gave up East and West Florida, and a new border followed the Sabine, Red and Arkansas rivers and then the line of 42° N to the Pacific. Before President Monroe's message of December 2, 1823, the United States had recognized four new nations, including Mexico on December 12, 1822. So the country went from fighting on its own borders to warning Europe to stay out of the Americas.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894

Answer notes: Land Cessions and Indian Removal, 1784–1894

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question
  • TopicAge of Jackson (also fits: Westward expansion and Manifest Destiny)
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.5(H)
    • FL SS.8.A.4.4

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

How did the United States gain American Indian land between 1784 and 1894, and why did the pattern change in the 1830s?

1. Notice: before 1830

With only Cessions dated before 1830 on, name states where the United States had gained land, one big empty part of the country, and the gaps in the Southeast.

Where to find it on the mapCessions dated before 1830 layer, The United States bookmark. Light blue covers most of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas and Florida, much of Alabama, Georgia and Tennessee, southern Michigan, the south and west of Mississippi, parts of Pennsylvania and New York, and land west of Missouri and Arkansas (today's Kansas and Oklahoma).

Accept answers that(a) Any three of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri, Arkansas, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, Mississippi (the south and west), southern Michigan, Kansas or Oklahoma. (b) The West, the upper Great Lakes and upper Mississippi (Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, northern Michigan), or the Atlantic coast. (c) Mississippi (north and center), Alabama (east-central and northeast) and Georgia (northwest).

NotesNew England and the states from New Jersey to South Carolina are empty or nearly empty because Royce's record starts with the federal government in 1784: land taken in colonial times, or by the states, isn't on this map. Central Florida is light blue because an 1823 treaty set it aside as a Seminole reservation, not because it was ceded then (see question 4). Both are questions about the source, which question 6 comes back to.

2. Predict

Before turning on the next layer, students predict where the cessions of the 1830s will be and give a reason. They write the prediction down first.

Accept answers thatAny prediction with a reason drawn from question 1: for example, the empty pockets in the Southeast surrounded by earlier cessions, the land next to the Great Lakes, or the West. Predictions are checked in question 3, not marked right or wrong here.

3. Reveal: the 1830s

Turn on Cessions dated 1830 to 1839 and compare the orange areas with the prediction. Use The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks.

Where to find it on the mapCessions dated 1830 to 1839 layer, with The Southeast and The Old Northwest bookmarks. Orange fills most of the empty pockets in the Southeast: northern and east-central Mississippi, east-central and northeastern Alabama with strips along the Mississippi border, northwest Georgia, and corners of Tennessee and North Carolina. It also covers central Florida, which was already light blue. In the north it covers most of Wisconsin, much of Iowa, northern Michigan and northern Indiana. About four tenths of the orange is west of the Mississippi, in Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska and Oklahoma.

Accept answers that(a) Any three of Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Wisconsin, Iowa, Michigan, Indiana, Florida, Kansas, Oklahoma, Missouri or Nebraska. (b) An honest comparison with the prediction. (c) The orange areas fill the gaps in Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia.

NotesSome orange areas in Kansas and Oklahoma were land assigned to nations moved west, which they ceded later; their pop-ups list more than one date. No question depends on them.

4. Explain why

Open orange cessions in the Southeast and read the nation, the date and the kind of document; use the Indian Removal Act (1830), in Before you start, to explain the pattern.

Where to find it on the mapCessions dated 1830 to 1839 layer, The Southeast bookmark, pop-ups. Mississippi, north-east of Jackson: Choctaw, September 27, 1830 (Today's states: Alabama, Mississippi). Alabama, north of Montgomery near the Georgia line: Creek, March 24, 1832. The north-west corner of Georgia: Cherokee, December 29, 1835 (Alabama, Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee). Others students may open: Chickasaw, October 20, 1832 (northern Mississippi); Seminole, central Florida around Orlando, September 18, 1823 and May 9, 1832. Each of these first links reads Treaty text. A student who clicks Jackson itself gets a light blue Choctaw cession of 1820.

Accept answers thatConnects the dates to the Indian Removal Act: after May 1830 the President could make removal treaties with nations east of the Mississippi, and within about five years the Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Cherokee nations had ceded their remaining homelands in Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia. Explains why here with Jackson's own reason: he wanted the land between Tennessee and Louisiana opened to white settlement, and these were the nations' remaining lands, surrounded by land already ceded. Strong answers note that the map shows when and where, and the documents give the why.

NotesTwo dates on one area don't always mean two cessions: Royce lists every treaty that concerns an area. The Seminole area in central Florida was set aside as a reservation in 1823 and ceded in 1832. The Treaty of New Echota (December 1835) was signed by the minority Treaty Party; Principal Chief John Ross, the Cherokee government and most Cherokees opposed it, and 3,352 Cherokees signed an 1836 petition asking the Senate not to ratify it (National Archives, DocsTeach). The National Archives says Jackson's administration negotiated almost 70 removal treaties, and nearly 50,000 people were moved to Indian Territory. Some people of each nation stayed in the Southeast: the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians (both in the pop-ups' Nations today) and the Poarch Band of Creek Indians in Alabama live there today.

5. Reveal: 1840 to 1894

Turn on Cessions dated 1840 to 1894 and describe how the pattern changed, using The Plains and the West bookmark.

Where to find it on the mapCessions dated 1840 to 1894 layer. Green covers almost all of the West: the Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the Southwest, California and the Pacific Northwest, and Minnesota. It also covers most of today's Oklahoma, where nations moved from the East later ceded land again. Still empty or nearly empty: New England, New Jersey to South Carolina (apart from parts of Pennsylvania and New York), most of Kentucky, most of Louisiana, eastern Texas and part of North Dakota.

Accept answers thatSays the cessions moved west of the Mississippi and across the whole West after 1840; notes the empty East and links it to the record starting in 1784.

NotesEastern Texas is empty; central and western Texas have cessions by the Comanche, Kiowa and Apache (1865 to 1886). Where several layers overlap (Oklahoma, Kansas, Iowa) the colors mix: clicking shows each area's dates.

6. Question the source

Read the note at the end of a pop-up and the Nations today line for two cessions, including the Creek cession of 1832, and ask whose view of these transactions the map shows.

Where to find it on the mapPop-up's last sentence: Royce compiled this from United States records (published 1899), so it shows how the federal government recorded the transaction, and the boundary is approximate. The Creek cession of March 24, 1832 reads "Not listed in this map's data." under Nations today.

Accept answers that(a) Charles Royce, from United States government records, published by the federal government in 1899. (b) A nation that exists today: the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in Oklahoma is one, and the Poarch Band of Creek Indians in Alabama another; the gap is in the modern data. (c) The pop-up records the Cherokee cession as a treaty, but the petition shows that many Cherokees said the people who signed it had no authority to speak for the nation, so the map gives the United States' side of a disputed agreement.

NotesThe petition is in the National Archives (Records of the U.S. Senate); DocsTeach has the image and transcription. The layer was digitized by the USDA Forest Service, which says the data are for information only, not for deciding title or boundaries.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer the compelling question with evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised for them. Accept answers that describe the pattern over time (the Ohio valley, much of the South and the land just west of the Mississippi before 1830; the Southeast and the upper Mississippi and Great Lakes in the 1830s; the West after 1840), connect the 1830s to the Indian Removal Act with dates from the pop-ups, and say that the map is a federal record. The students' own questions are a good place to start the next lesson, for example on the Trail of Tears.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use all three layers in order (where light blue, orange and green fall), pop-up names and dates for at least two 1830s Southeast cessions (Choctaw, September 27, 1830; Creek, March 24, 1832; Cherokee, December 29, 1835), the Indian Removal Act and Jackson's reason, and the pop-up's note on who recorded the map.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

The United States gained most of this land by treaty, and the cessions moved across the map in order. Before 1830 the light blue covers Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Missouri and much of the South, but there are gaps in Mississippi, Alabama and northwest Georgia. When I turned on the orange 1830s layer, those gaps filled in. The pop-ups show the Choctaw cession on September 27, 1830, the Creek on March 24, 1832 and the Cherokee on December 29, 1835. The Indian Removal Act of May 1830 let the President make removal treaties, and Jackson wanted that land opened to white settlers. After 1840 the green layer covers almost the whole West. The map was made from United States records, so it shows the government's side. In 1836 thousands of Cherokees signed a petition saying their treaty was made without the nation's authority.

Standards
