C3 D2.Geo.2.6-8Framework: C3 FrameworkStandard: Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics.

TX 8.10(A)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
TX 8.5(H)Framework: Texas TEKSStandard: Analyze the reasons for the removal and resettlement of Cherokee Indians during the Jacksonian era, including the Indian Removal Act, Worcester v. Georgia, and the Trail of Tears (partial: this lesson covers the Indian Removal Act and reasons from Jackson's 1830 message and the 1836 Cherokee petition; Worcester v. Georgia is a resource only, and the Trail of Tears is planned for a later map).
FL SS.8.A.4.4Framework: FloridaStandard: Discuss the impact of westward expansion on cultural practices and migration patterns of Native Americans, African slave populations and other minority groups (partial: the migration of Native Americans; not cultural practices).

pages.summary: Where to find each answer on the map and what to accept, for the MapMaker lesson The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote. For teachers.

settings.markdown:
Lessons › The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote

Answer notes: The Election of 1828 and the Right to Vote

For teachers. This page holds the answers and what to accept. With students, share the lesson page or the map, not this page.
  • Grade8
  • TimeAbout 60 minutes over two class periods: questions 1 to 4, then 5, 6 and the big question
  • TopicAge of Jackson
  • Student loginNot needed to explore the map
  • Standards
    • C3 D2.Civ.2.6-8
    • C3 D2.His.14.6-8
    • TX 8.10(A)
    • TX 8.5(G)

Open in MapMaker (opens in a new tab) Lesson page Download Word (teacher notes)

Answer notes

Compelling question

Andrew Jackson's election in 1828 is often called a victory for the common man. Who could vote in 1828, and did it depend on where you lived?

1. Notice: the result

With only the votes layer on, find which states voted for Jackson and which for Adams, and the states that split.

Where to find it on the mapElection of 1828: electors' votes layer, legend and pop-ups. All orange: Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Vermont. All blue: the South and the West (Alabama, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia) and Pennsylvania. Split: New York (Jackson 20, Adams 16), Maryland (Jackson 5, Adams 6) and Maine (Jackson 1, Adams 8).

Accept answers that(a) Adams: New England and nearby New Jersey and Delaware. Jackson: the South and the West, plus Pennsylvania. (b) New York, Maryland and Maine.

NotesTotals, not on the map: Jackson 178, Adams 83 (National Archives).

2. Predict

Before turning on the voting-rule layers, students predict where white men had to own property or pay a tax to vote, and where free Black men could vote, with a reason. They write the prediction down first.

Accept answers thatAny prediction with a reason, for example that the older coastal states kept older rules, or that newer western states were more open. Predictions are checked in questions 3 and 4, not marked right or wrong here.

3. Reveal: white men

Turn on White men and the vote, 1828 and compare the shading with the prediction and with the votes.

Where to find it on the mapWhite men and the vote, 1828 layer. Dark (had to own property): Virginia and Rhode Island. Light (no rule): Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, New York, Maryland, Kentucky, Tennessee, Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri, and South Carolina for state elections. Middle (pay a tax): Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio, Mississippi and Louisiana.

Accept answers that(a) Virginia and Rhode Island; also accept North Carolina with the reason that its state Senate voters needed 50 acres. (b) About half are newer states west of the Appalachian Mountains (Kentucky, Tennessee, Indiana, Illinois, Alabama, Missouri); the others are Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont and New York in the North, and Maryland and South Carolina. (c) No: Jackson won Virginia, where white men had to own property, and several tax states; Adams won states with no rule (Vermont, New Hampshire, most of Maine and Maryland) as well as Rhode Island. The rules and the result don't line up neatly.

NotesNew York's 1821 constitution eased the rules for white men and an 1826 amendment removed what was left. Virginia's property rule was loosened by a new constitution in 1830. Delaware's and South Carolina's rules were for state elections: their legislatures chose the electors. In South Carolina and Tennessee a man could qualify by owning land or by living in the area six months, so no property was needed.

4. Reveal: free Black men

Turn off the white men layer and turn on Free Black men and the vote, 1828; compare with question 3.

Where to find it on the mapFree Black men and the vote, 1828 layer and pop-ups. Light green (could vote on the same terms): Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, North Carolina (until 1835) and Tennessee (until 1834). Middle green: New York (the 1821 constitution set a new rule for Black men only: own property worth $250, pay tax on it and have been a citizen for three years) and Pennsylvania (the law didn't mention race, but in many places officials kept Black men from voting). Dark green (could not vote): the other 16 states.

Accept answers that(a) Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, Massachusetts, North Carolina and Tennessee. (b) White men in New York had no property or tax rule after 1826, but Black men had to own $250 of property. (c) All four shut out free Black men: in these states voting was opened to more white men while Black men were kept out. Tennessee, also west of the Appalachians, is the exception: free Black men could vote there until 1834.

NotesIn 1825 only 298 Black men in the whole state of New York met the $250 rule (Peter J. Galie, Albany Law Review, citing Phyllis Field; Galie gives nearly 6,000 free adult Black New Yorkers). Before 1821 New York's property rules were the same for all voters. Free Black men lost the vote in North Carolina in 1835 and in Tennessee under its 1834 constitution.

5. Explain why

Read the pop-ups for South Carolina and Delaware (the legislature chose electors) and Georgia (voters chose them for the first time); explain what that meant for who could vote for president.

Where to find it on the mapPop-ups. South Carolina and Delaware: the state legislature chose the electors, so voters had no direct say. Georgia: voters chose the electors for the first time (the legislature chose in 1824); Louisiana's and Vermont's pop-ups say the same.

Accept answers that(a) The state legislature. (b) Voters chose the electors for the first time. (c) No: even men who could vote in state elections had no direct vote for president there, because the legislature chose the electors. So who could vote for president depended on how a state chose its electors as well as on its rules for voters. In Georgia, Louisiana and Vermont voters chose the electors for the first time in 1828, which is part of what expanded suffrage meant.

NotesEvery pop-up says: "Women could not vote in any state in 1828." New Jersey had ended women's voting in 1807.

6. Question the source

Students ask what the map can and can't show: it shows the rules in law, not who actually voted.

Where to find it on the mapPennsylvania pop-up: the constitution didn't mention race, but in many places, Philadelphia among them, officials kept Black men from voting; a new constitution shut them out in 1838. Every pop-up: women could not vote in any state in 1828.

Accept answers that(a) The law allowed Black men to vote, but officials kept many from voting. (b) Enslaved people, and people in the territories, who couldn't vote for president; women appear only in the note that they could not vote. (c) Popular vote counts by state, newspapers, poll records or diaries: the map shows the rules, not who turned out.

Answering the compelling question

Students answer with evidence from all three layers and at least two pop-ups, then write one "why" question the map raised. Accept answers that say who could vote depended on the state, name the property states (Virginia and Rhode Island) and the tax states, note that free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men in only six states and women in none, and weigh the 'common man' description: more white men could vote, and many people could not.

Assessing the answer

One way to assess the answer to the compelling question: the rubric every lesson shares (four criteria, four levels), with this lesson's own line on what counts as map evidence, and a model answer at the top level. Use it as it is, adapt it, or use your own.

Map evidence in this lessonStrong answers use the pies (Adams in New England, Jackson in the South and West, three split states), the white men layer (Virginia and Rhode Island property, the tax states, the light states), the free Black men layer (six states, New York's $250 rule) and the pop-ups' note on women.

Criterion1 Beginning2 Developing3 Secure4 Strong
Claim1 Beginning: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.2 Developing: Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.3 Secure: Gives a clear answer to the big question.4 Strong: Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).
Map evidence1 Beginning: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.2 Developing: One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).3 Secure: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.4 Strong: Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.
Geographic reasoning1 Beginning: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.2 Developing: Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.3 Secure: Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.4 Strong: Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.
Accuracy1 Beginning: Several facts do not match the map.2 Developing: Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.3 Secure: Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.4 Strong: Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.

A model answer (level 4)

Who could vote in 1828 depended a lot on where you lived. In the votes layer, Adams won New England and Jackson won the South and the West, but the voting rules don't follow that split. When I turned on the white men layer, Virginia and Rhode Island were dark green, so a white man there had to own property, while in Indiana, Illinois and Alabama there was no property or tax rule. Jackson won Virginia anyway. The free Black men layer showed that free Black men could vote on the same terms as white men in only six states, and Indiana, Illinois, Alabama and Missouri shut them out. New York's pop-up says white men had no property rule after 1826, but Black men had to own $250 of property. Every pop-up also says women could not vote in any state. So 1828 was a victory for more white men, but not for everyone the common man might include.

Standards
